paragraphs.text: Of Our Father among the Saints, the Bishop of Nyssa: On the Life of Moses, or On Perfection in Virtue.

Think of what happens to people who love watching horse races. The horses they back in the contests on the track may lack nothing in eagerness or speed, yet in their zeal for victory the spectators still shout down from the stands, following the race around with their eyes. They urge the charioteer on (or so they think) to a sharper charge, calling out to the horses as well, and stretching out and waving their hands at them in place of a whip. They do this not because it achieves anything

but out of goodwill toward the contestants, showing their eagerness by voice and gesture. Something like this, it seems to me, is what I myself am doing in your case, most honored of my friends and brothers. You are competing nobly in the stadium of virtue, running the divine race, and straining toward the prize of the upward calling with quick, light strides; and I call out to you, spur you on, and urge you to put still more effort into your speed. I do this not because some irrational enthusiasm carries me away, but to give pleasure to a beloved child. For the letter you sent me recently conveyed this request: that we should give you some counsel about the perfect life. I thought it right to provide it. Perhaps nothing else in what I say will be of use to you, but this at least will surely not be useless: that it gives you an example of ready obedience. For if we, who have been set in the rank of fathers over so many souls, think it fitting at our gray-haired age to accept a command from a sober-minded youth, how much more fitting is it that the achievement of obedience be confirmed in you, since we ourselves trained your youth in willing obedience. But enough of that. We must now set our hand to the task before us, taking God as the guide of our discourse. You asked, dear friend, that we sketch out for you what the perfect life is. Clearly you had this in view: if what you are seeking were found in our discourse, you might carry over into your own life the grace the discourse revealed. But I am equally at a loss on both counts. To grasp perfection in words, and to show in one's life what the mind has perceived — each of these, I declare, is beyond my power. And perhaps not I alone, but many great men who excel in virtue will admit that such a thing is out of their reach. So that I may not seem, in the Psalmist's words, to fear a fear where there is no fear, I will set out more clearly what I mean. In all other things that are measured by the senses, perfection is contained within certain fixed limits, as with quantity, whether continuous or discrete. Every measure of quantity is enclosed by its own boundaries, and anyone who looks at a cubit or at the number ten knows that it begins at one point and ends at another, and that in this lies its being perfect. But in the case of virtue we have learned from the Apostle that its one limit of perfection is that it has no limit. For that great and lofty-minded man, the divine Apostle, as he ran the course of virtue, never stopped straining toward what lay ahead, since to halt in the race was not safe for him. Why? Because every good, by its own nature, has no limit, but is limited only by being set against its opposite: as life is limited by death, and light by darkness. In general, every good comes to an end at whatever is understood as the opposite of the good. For just as the end of life is the beginning of death, so too halting in the race of virtue

becomes the beginning of the race of vice. So our statement was not false when it said that perfection in virtue cannot be grasped, for it has been shown that whatever is enclosed by limits is not virtue. I also said that it is impossible even for those who pursue the life of virtue to attain perfection, and this point too will now be made clear. The primary and proper Good, whose very nature is goodness, is the Divine itself; whatever it is conceived to be by nature, that it both is and is called. Now it has been shown that virtue has no limit except vice, and the Divine does not admit its opposite. Therefore the divine nature is understood to be unbounded and without limit. But whoever pursues true virtue participates in nothing other than God, because he is himself complete virtue. Since, then, what is good by nature is wholly desirable to those who know it, so that they long to share in it, and since this good has no limit, the desire of the one who shares in it must necessarily stretch out along with the limitless and never come to a halt. It is therefore altogether impossible to attain perfection, because perfection, as has been said, is not enclosed by limits, and the one limit of virtue is limitlessness. How, then, could anyone reach the limit he seeks, when he cannot find any limit? Yet even though our argument has shown that what we seek is wholly beyond our grasp, we must not neglect the Lord's commandment, which says: "Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect." For in things that are good by nature, even if it is not possible to attain the whole, not to miss out on a part would be a great gain, at least for those with any sense. We must therefore show all zeal not to fall entirely short of the perfection that is possible, but to acquire as much of it as we have room to see of what we seek. For perhaps the perfection of human nature is just this: to be so disposed as always to want more of the good. I think it right to take Scripture as our counselor on this. For the divine voice says somewhere through the prophecy of Isaiah: "Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah who bore you in travail." The word surely gives this command to those who are wandering outside virtue. Sailors at sea who have been carried off the straight course to harbor bring themselves back from their wandering by some sign that appears, either a beacon fire they see raised up on a height or the peak of some mountain coming into view. In the same way, the word uses the example of Sarah and Abraham to steer back toward the harbor of the divine will those who drift on the sea of life with no pilot for their minds. For human nature is divided into female and male, and the choice between virtue and vice lies open equally to both, by their own free will. For this reason the divine voice has shown each part a fitting example of virtue, so that each might look to what is akin to it — the men to Abraham, the other part to Sarah — and both might be guided by their own examples toward the life of virtue. Perhaps, then, it would be enough

for us too if the memory of one of those who won renown for their lives served as our beacon, and showed us how the soul can be brought to anchor in the calm harbor of virtue, never tossed by the storms of life nor shipwrecked in the depths of vice by the rolling waves of the passions, one after another. Perhaps that is why the conduct of those exalted men has been recorded in such detail: so that later generations, by imitating those who succeeded before them, might direct their lives toward the good. "What then?" someone will say. "I am not a Chaldean, as Abraham is recorded to have been, nor was I raised by the Egyptian's daughter, as the account tells of Moses. In such matters my life has nothing at all corresponding to any of the ancients. How shall I put myself in the same rank as one of them, when I have no way of imitating, in my own pursuits, someone so far removed from me?" To him we shall reply that we do not judge virtue or vice by whether someone is a Chaldean. No one is banished from the life of virtue by living in Egypt or dwelling in Babylon; nor, again, is God known to the worthy [only] in Judea; nor is Zion, in the obvious sense, the dwelling place of God. Rather, we need a subtler understanding and keener sight to discern from the history what kind of Chaldeans or Egyptians we must leave far behind, and from what kind of Babylonian captivity we must be set free, if we are to lay hold of the most blessed life. Let Moses, then, be set before us in our discourse as a pattern of life. First we will run briefly through his life as we have learned it from the divine voice; then we will look for the meaning that fits the history, as counsel for virtue, and through it we shall come to know the life that is perfect, so far as that is possible for human beings. It is said, then, that Moses was born at a time when the tyrant's law forbade male infants to be kept alive, yet by grace he already possessed all that time would later have added. From his swaddling clothes he was seen to be a beautiful child, and this made his parents shrink from doing away with such a child by death. Then, when the tyrant's threat grew too strong, he was not simply thrown into the stream of the Nile. Instead he was placed in a basket whose joints had been smeared with bitumen and pitch, and so committed to the current (this is what those who carefully recorded his story have related). A divine power steered the basket, and it came to rest against a bank off to the side, the motion of the waves washing it up there of its own accord. The king's daughter happened to be walking through the meadows on that bank when the basket ran aground, and he became her find, crying like a baby in the chest. When she saw him, with the grace that shone about him, he at once won the princess's affection and was taken up into

the rank of a son. But since he naturally turned away from a foreign breast, through the plan of one of his kinsfolk he was nursed at his own mother's breast. When he had passed the age of childhood, raised in the royal household and educated in the learning of outsiders, which outsiders held in esteem, he no longer chose to acknowledge as his mother that learned woman by whom he had been adopted as a son. Instead he returned to his natural mother and joined himself to his own people. When a fight broke out between a Hebrew and an Egyptian, he took the side of his kinsman and killed the foreigner. Then, when two Hebrews came to blows with each other, he tried to calm their quarrel, advising them that, since they were brothers, they should make nature the arbiter of their disputes, not anger. Rebuffed by the one who was bent on wrongdoing [?], he made this dishonor the occasion for a higher philosophy. Withdrawing far from life among the crowd, he lived in solitude from then on, and became the son-in-law of a foreigner, a man with an eye for what was better and practiced at judging the character and life of men. From a single action — I mean his attack on the shepherds — this man saw the young man's virtue: he had fought for what was right without regard to his own gain, but because he held justice precious in its own nature, and so had punished the injustice of shepherds who had done him no wrong at all. The man admired the young man for this, and judging his virtue, in its apparent poverty, more precious than wealth of many talents, he gave him his daughter in marriage and left him free to pursue the life he desired. His was a life in the mountains and in solitude, free from all the bustle of the marketplace, as he lived apart in the wilderness tending the sheep. After some time had passed in this way of life, the history says, a fearful theophany came to him at high noon, when a light other than the sun's flashed all around his eyes. Astonished at the strange sight, he looked up toward the mountain and saw a bush from which the radiance blazed out like fire, while the branches of the bush kept flourishing in the flame as if in dew. And he said these words to himself: "I will go over and see this great sight." When he had said this, he no longer received the wonder of the light with his eyes alone. Instead, most astonishing of all, his hearing too was lit up by the rays of that radiance. For the grace of the light was divided between both senses: it flooded his eyes with the brilliance of its rays and enlightened his hearing with pure teachings. So the voice of that light forbids Moses to approach the mountain weighed down by dead sandals; he must loose the sandals from his feet and only then touch that ground lit up by the divine light. After this (for I think we should not linger too long over the bare history of the man, so that our words may keep to the subject at hand), strengthened by the theophany he had seen, he is commanded to rescue his own people from slavery to the Egyptians. And so that he might learn above all the strength that was coming into him from God, he makes a trial, at the divine

command, with what he held in his hands. The trial was this. A rod fell from his hand, came to life, and became a living creature (the creature was a serpent); and when his hand took it up again, it became what it had been before it turned into a beast. And his hand, when he drew it out of his bosom, was changed to the whiteness of snow; when he put it back inside again, it returns to its own nature. As Moses was going down to Egypt, bringing with him his foreign wife and the children she had borne him, an angel is said to have met him, bringing the fear of death, which the woman appeased with the blood of her child's circumcision. Then comes the meeting with Aaron, who had also been moved by God to go and meet him. After this the two of them gather the people in Egypt into a common assembly, and deliverance from slavery is proclaimed to those already worn out by the misery of their labors, and he addresses the tyrant himself. At this the tyrant's anger grows greater than before, both against the overseers of the works and against the Israelites themselves. The quota of bricks is increased, and a harsher order is sent down, so that they now suffered not only with the clay but also toiled over chaff and straw. Pharaoh (for that was the name of the tyrant of the Egyptians) tried to counter with trickery, through the craft of sorcerers, the signs that Moses performed by God's power. When Moses once more turned his rod into a beast before the eyes of the Egyptians, the sorcery was thought to work an equal wonder with the magicians' rods. But the trick was exposed by what happened. The serpent that had been changed from Moses' rod devoured the sorcerers' sticks — the supposed snakes — and so showed that the sorcerers' rods had no power either to defend themselves or to live, but only the outward shape that the sorcery had cunningly displayed to the eyes of the easily deceived. Then Moses, seeing that all the subjects were of one mind with the leader of wickedness, brings a common plague on the whole Egyptian nation, sparing no one from the experience of evils. In this onslaught against the Egyptians, the very elements of existing things that we see in the universe — earth and fire, air and water — moved along with him like an army under his command, changing their operations according to the moral choice of each person. For by the same power, at the same time and in the same place, the lawless were punished while those free from vice remained unharmed. When all the water in Egypt was turned into blood at Moses' command, so that even the fish died as the water changed into a fleshy thickness, for the Hebrews alone the blood they drew was water. This is how the sorcery found occasion to counterfeit the bloody appearance, using the water found among the Hebrews. Likewise, when frogs swarmed over Egypt in a mass (their generation did not pour forth in such numbers by any normal course of nature; rather, the command itself brought into being a new kind of creature that appeared then in the frogs), the whole Egyptian population was being ruined, hemmed in by these creatures in their homes, while the life of the Hebrews remained clean of this nuisance. So too the air gave the Egyptians

no distinction between night and day, as they remained in unbroken gloom, while for the Hebrews nothing in all this departed from the usual. And all the rest worked in the same way — the hail, the fire, the boils, the gnats, the dog-flies, the cloud of locusts: each acted against the Egyptians according to its nature, while the Hebrews learned of their neighbors' suffering only through reports and stories, and suffered no attack from such things themselves. Then the destruction of the firstborn drew the line between Hebrew and Egyptian more sharply still. The one people were overwhelmed with lamentation at the loss of those dearest to them, while the others remained in complete quiet and safety. Their deliverance was made secure by blood poured out at every entrance, the doorposts on either side, together with the lintel joining them, being marked with the blood. While the Egyptians lay stricken by the disaster of the firstborn, each lamenting his sufferings privately and all lamenting them together, Moses leads the Israelites out in the exodus. He had prepared them beforehand to take the wealth of the Egyptians with them, under the pretext of borrowing it. When they had gone three days' journey out of Egypt, the history says, the Egyptian once again took it badly that Israel had not stayed in slavery. He equipped all his subjects for war and charged against the people with his cavalry. When the people saw the array of horses and weapons, being inexperienced in war and unused to such sights, they were at once struck with fear and turned against Moses. At this point the history tells the most astonishing thing about Moses. He was divided in two in what he did: with his voice and words he encouraged the Israelites and urged them to keep up good hope, while inwardly, in his mind, he brought a plea to God on behalf of the terrified people. And he was guided by counsel from above as to how to escape the danger, God himself (as the history says) hearing his silent cry. A cloud led the people by divine power. It was not of ordinary nature: it was not formed from vapors or exhalations, with the air thickened by vapors into a misty mass and pressed together by the winds. It was something better and higher than human understanding. As Scripture testifies, the wonder of that cloud was such that when the sun's rays blazed down hotly, it was a protecting wall for the people, shading what lay beneath and cooling the fiery air with a fine dew; and through the night it became fire, lighting the Israelites' way with its own light from evening until dawn. Moses himself looked to it and taught the people to follow what appeared. When they came to the Red Sea, where the cloud was leading them on their journey, the Egyptians with their whole army closed in on the people from behind, and no escape from danger was left to them on any side, trapped as they were between enemies and water. Then Moses, moved by divine power, accomplished the most incredible thing of all. Approaching the water at the shore, he strikes the sea with his rod, and at the blow it split apart. And just as with glass it is natural

…to run right through it: if a crack starts at any point, it runs straight across to the far edge. In the same way, when that whole sea was split by the rod at its edge, the breaking of the waters also ran across to the opposite shore. Moses went down into the depths where the sea had been cut through, and with all the people he was at the bottom of the sea, yet his body stayed dry and in the sunlight. He crossed the abyss on foot over the dry floor of the sea, and he did not fear that sudden wall-building of the waves, as the salt water stood fixed on either side of them, to the right and to the left, like a wall. But when Pharaoh and the Egyptians rushed into the sea after them along that newly opened road through the waters, the water joined with the water again. The sea flowed back on itself into its former shape, and there was once more a single, unbroken surface of water. By then the Israelites were on the far shore, resting from the long and strenuous march through the sea. There they sang a song of victory to God, who had raised for them that day a bloodless trophy, since the whole Egyptian army, men, horses, weapons and chariots alike, had been wiped out by the water. Then Moses went on further, and after a three days' march through waterless country he was at a loss, with no way to relieve the army's thirst. For there was a lake beside which they had camped, but its water was like seawater, or rather more bitter than the sea. So as they sat beside the water and burned with thirst for water, Moses received counsel from God: he found a piece of wood near the place and threw it into the water, and at once the water was drinkable, for the wood by its own power changed the nature of the water from bitterness to sweetness. When the cloud moved on ahead, they too moved on with the movement of their guide. They always did this: they halted their march wherever the cloud, by stopping, gave the signal to rest, and they set out again wherever the cloud led their march. Following this guide, they came to a place well watered with drinkable water, abundantly washed by twelve springs. There were also seventy palm trees, which, few as they were, were enough to make a great marvel for those who saw them, because they surpassed others in beauty and size. From there too the guiding cloud roused the army and led it to another place. This was a desert of parched and scorching sand, with no water to moisten the ground. There, when thirst again wore the people down, a rock on a hill was struck by Moses with his rod and gave out sweet, drinkable water, more than enough for the needs of so great a people. It was there too that the store of food which they had brought with them from Egypt for the journey ran out, and as the people were pressed by hunger, the most incredible thing of all happened: their food did not appear from the earth in the usual way, but flowed down from heaven above like dew. For dew was poured out on them at daybreak, and the dew became food for those who gathered it. What was poured out was not a watery drop, as is usual with dew, but instead crystal-like grains, shaped like what is commonly called coriander, the seed of the coriander plant, came down formed into little spheres, and their taste imitated the sweetness of honey.

Along with this marvel another was also seen. All went out to gather it, people of different ages and strengths, as one would expect, yet no one brought in less than another because of a difference in strength; what was gathered was measured by each person's need, so that the stronger did not have more and the weaker did not fall short of an equal share. In addition to this the history tells of another marvel: each person took enough for the day and stored nothing for the next. If anyone out of thrift saved some of the day's food, what was stored up was useless as food, for it turned into worms. There is yet another wonder in the account of this food. One of the days of the week was honored with rest from work, for some mystical reason. On the day before it, although the same amount fell as at other times and the eagerness of the gatherers was the same, what was gathered was found to be double the usual measure, so that they would have no excuse to break the law of rest because they needed food. In this the divine power was shown even more, because on the other days whatever was left over became useless, but only on the day of preparation before the Sabbath (for that is the name of the day of rest) did what was stored remain unspoiled, so that it seemed in no way staler than fresh food. Then a war broke out between them and a foreign nation (the account names those who rose against them at that time Amalekites). Then for the first time the Israelites armed themselves for battle. Not all of them were mustered for the fight in full force; rather, the best were picked out, and the choice men among them took up the war. Here again Moses showed a new kind of generalship. For while Joshua, who led the people after Moses, was leading the army out against the Amalekites, Moses, away from the fighting, looked up to heaven from a lookout on a hill, with two of his close companions standing on either side of him. At that point we hear from the history of the following marvel concerning what happened. Whenever Moses lifted his hands toward heaven, his followers gained strength against the enemy; but whenever he lowered them, the army gave way before the attack of the foreigners. When those standing beside him understood this, since Moses' hands had become heavy and hard to move for some hidden reason, they came up on either side and held them up. But since they were too weak to keep him upright, they propped up his seat with a stone, and so by their help they enabled Moses to raise his hands to heaven. When this was done, the foreigners were decisively defeated by the Israelites. Since the cloud which led the people on their march stayed in the same place, the people necessarily did not move either, as nothing led them to move on. And so they had abundant means of living without toil: from the air above bread rained down ready for them, from the rock below drink was supplied, and the cloud relieved the discomforts of living in the open, so that it became a wall of shelter against the heat

by day, and by night it dispelled the darkness, shining with a fiery light. Thus their stay in that desert at the foot of the mountain, where the camp was set up, was free of hardship. During this time Moses also led them into a more secret initiation, as the divine power itself, through marvels beyond reason, initiated both the whole people and their leader himself. This initiation was carried out in the following way. The people had been told beforehand to keep clear of every other defilement seen in body and soul, to purify themselves with certain sprinklings, and also to abstain even from marriage for a set number of days, so that, washed clean of every passionate and bodily disposition, they might approach the mountain free of passion to be initiated. The name of the mountain was Sinai. At that time only rational beings were permitted to climb it, and of these only men, and of these again only those purified from every defilement. Every guard and precaution was taken that no irrational creature should set foot on the mountain; and if one ever did, whatever of irrational nature appeared on the mountain was to be stoned by the people. Then the light of the air, after a clear sky, was blackened with gloom, so that the mountain became invisible, surrounded on every side by the darkness. Fire shining out of the darkness made a frightening sight for those who saw it, as it spread over the whole circuit of the mountain, so that everything visible smoldered with smoke from the fire running beneath. Moses led the people in the ascent, yet he himself was not confident at what he saw. His soul cowered in fear and his body trembled with terror, so that he did not even hide the state of his soul from the Israelites, but admitted to them that he was terrified by what appeared and could not keep his body still. For what appeared was not merely of a kind to strike the soul with terror through the eyes; frightening things also resounded through the ears, as a voice from above broke terrifyingly over everything below. Its very first onset was harsh and unbearable to every ear. It resembled the sound of trumpets, but it surpassed every such comparison in its fearsome and terrifying power. As it went on it grew more fearful, always raising its sound to a still more terrifying pitch. This voice was articulate: by divine power, without organs of speech, the air itself articulated the words. And the words were not articulated at random; they laid down divine teachings as law. As the voice went on it grew ever stronger, and the trumpet outsounded itself, each later blast always surpassing the earlier ones. The whole people were too weak to bear what they saw and heard. So a common request from all of them was brought to Moses, that the law be conveyed through him as mediator, since the people would not doubt that whatever he commanded according to the teaching from above

was a divine command. So when all of them had run back down to the foot of the mountain, Moses was left alone, and he showed in himself the opposite of what he had been. For while all the others, in the company of those who shared their experience, were rather more confident in the face of these terrors, he, once left alone, was bolder than those who had stood with him. From this it became clear that the fear which had gripped him at first was not his own feeling, but that he had felt it out of sympathy for those who were terrified. So, stripped of the people's cowardice as of a kind of burden, he was on his own. Then he dared to enter the darkness itself, and he went within the invisible, no longer seen by those watching [for, having slipped into the unspeakable depth of the divine initiation, he was there with the Invisible, himself unseen]. By what he did he taught, I think, that anyone who means to be with God must go beyond everything visible and, lifting up his mind to the invisible and incomprehensible as to the summit of a mountain, believe that the divine is there where understanding does not reach. When he was there, he received the divine commands. These were a teaching of virtue, whose chief point is piety, that is, holding fitting conceptions about the divine nature: that it transcends every concept and image of knowledge and is like nothing that is known. For it commands that in our conceptions of God we look to nothing that can be grasped, and not liken the nature that transcends all things to anything known by comprehension, but, believing that it is, leave unsearched what it is like, how great, from where, or how it is, since that is beyond reach. The word adds also the right conduct of moral life, giving its teaching in general and particular laws. In general there is the law that does away with all injustice: that one must have love toward one's own kind. Once this is established, it follows as a matter of course that no one does any harm to his neighbor. Among the particular laws, honor toward parents is prescribed, and the list of forbidden offenses is enumerated. Having had his mind, as it were, purified beforehand by these laws, he was led on to a more perfect initiation, as a tabernacle was suddenly shown to him by divine power. The tabernacle was a temple whose beauty lay in a variety hard to describe: entrance gateways, pillars and curtains, a table and lampstand, an altar of incense, an altar and a mercy seat, and, within the holy places, the inner sanctuary which no one might enter. So that the beauty and arrangement of all these might not slip from memory, and that the marvel might be shown to those below, he was advised not to record them in mere writing, but to imitate that immaterial workmanship by a material construction, taking the most splendid and brilliant materials found on earth. Of these there was mostly gold, overlaid all round the pillars. With the gold silver was also used, adorning the capitals and bases of the pillars, so that, I think, the gold, set off on either side by the contrasting color, might shine all the more. In some places bronze too was thought useful, serving as capital and base for the silver columns. The veils and curtains, the enclosure of the temple, and the roof stretched over the pillars [Exod. 25:18]

were all made fittingly by the weaver's skill, each from the appropriate material. For some of the woven fabrics there was blue dye, and purple, and the fiery gleam of scarlet, and the brightness of fine linen in its natural, unworked appearance. For others, flax was used, and for others hair, according to the purpose of the weaving. In some places red-dyed skins were also suited to the beauty of the structure. These things Moses had made by his assistants after his descent from the mountain, following the pattern of the workmanship that had been shown to him. But at that time, while he was within that temple not made with hands, he was given laws about the adornment with which the priest must be made splendid when he enters the inner sanctuary, as the word laid down each detail of both the inner vesture and the outer. The vesture begins not with what is hidden but with what is visible. There was an ephod, embroidered in various dyes, the same from which the veil was made, but with more gold thread. There were clasps on either side holding the ephod together, setting emeralds in gold all round. The stones' natural adornment was their brilliance, which flashed green rays from itself, and their artificial adornment was the marvel of their engraving. The craft did not carve the image of any idols; rather, the names of the patriarchs, six on each stone, were engraved on them and served as their adornment. Then there were the little shields hanging from them on the front, and the chains interwoven with one another in alternation, in a regular pattern, plaited like a net, hanging down from the clasp on either side above the shields, so that, I think, the beauty of the plaiting might shine out more, set off by what lay beneath it. There was also that golden ornament placed over the breast, in which were set stones of various kinds, equal in number to the patriarchs, arranged in four rows of three each, showing in letters on themselves the names of the founders of the tribes. There was the robe beneath the ephod, reaching from the neck to the feet, handsomely adorned with hanging tassels. Its lower hem was made beautiful not only by the variety of the weaving but also by pendants of gold. These were golden bells and pomegranates, set alternately around the lower hem. Then there was the headband, all blue, and the plate on the forehead, of pure gold, engraved with an unspeakable inscription. There was a belt which gathered in the loose folds of the vesture, the adornment of the hidden parts, and all the other things by which, in the form of vesture, instruction about priestly virtue is given in riddles. When he had been taught such things in God's secret teaching, enveloped in that invisible darkness, and had become greater than himself by the addition of the mystical lessons, he came up out of the darkness again and went down to his own people, to share with

them the marvels shown to him in the theophany, to deliver the laws, and to establish for the people the temple and the priesthood according to the pattern shown to him on the mountain. He also carried in his hands the sacred tablets, which were a divine discovery and gift and needed no cooperation to be made; both alike were the work of God, the material and the writing engraved on it. But the people thwarted the grace before the lawgiver arrived, by running wild into idolatry. For Moses had spent no short time occupied in converse with God through that divine initiation: for forty days and as many nights he shared in that eternal life beneath the darkness, and he went beyond nature itself (for during that time his body needed no food). Then the people, like a youngster out of sight of his tutor, were carried away by senseless impulses into disorder. They rose against Aaron and forced the priest to lead them in idolatry. When the idol had been made out of gold (the idol was a calf), they exulted in their impiety. But Moses, now reaching them, broke the tablets which he was bringing from God, so that they might suffer a punishment worthy of their offense, deprived of the grace that God had given. Then, having purged the pollution by the blood of their kinsmen through the Levites, propitiated God by his own anger against those who had sinned, and destroyed the idol, he again received tablets after waiting forty days. Their writing was by divine power, but their material was worked by the hand of Moses. He received these again after going beyond nature for that same number of days, living in another way and not in the way customary for us, and taking into his body nothing of the food that supports the neediness of our nature. And so he set up the tabernacle for them, delivered the ordinances, and established the priesthood according to the teaching given him by God. And when he had built everything through material workmanship according to the divine guidance — the tabernacle, the entrance gateways, everything inside, the censers, the altar, the lampstand, the curtains, the mercy seat within the inner sanctuary, the priestly adornment, the ointment, the various sacred rites, the purifications, the thank offerings, the offerings to avert evils, the propitiatory offerings for sins — having arranged them all among them in the proper manner, he stirred up against himself among those close to him envy, that sickness innate in human nature. As a result, Aaron, though honored with the dignities of the priesthood, and his sister Miriam, moved by a somewhat womanish jealousy at the honor given him by God, said something for which God was provoked to punish the offense. Here Moses is even more to be admired for his forbearance: when God was punishing the woman's senseless envy, he made his nature stronger than his anger and propitiated God on behalf of his sister. When the multitude again turned to disorder (the offense was led by an immoderate desire for the pleasures of the belly: it was not enough for them to live healthily and without hardship on the food that flowed down from above, but their craving for flesh and longing for meat made slavery among the Egyptians preferable to the good things they had), he consulted God

about the passion that had broken out among them. But he teaches them that they ought not to be so disposed by letting them obtain what they longed for. He sent upon the camp a great number of birds, flying close to the ground like a cloud and swooping down on it in flocks. The ease of catching them carried their craving for meat to the point of surfeit. But the excess of eating suddenly turned the temperament of their bodies into corrupting humors, and their glut ended in sickness and death. Their example was enough to teach self-restraint both to those men themselves and to all who looked at them. Next, spies are sent by him into the land that, according to God's promise, they hoped to inhabit. Not all of them brought back a true report; some announced false and gloomy things, and once again the people turned their anger on Moses. God condemns those who had despaired of his help never to see the land promised to them. As they went on through the desert, the water failed them again, and with it their memory of God's power also failed. For the earlier miracle at the rock did not persuade them that their need would not go unmet now either. Abandoning better hopes, they went so far as to revile God himself and Moses, so that even Moses seemed to give way under the people's unbelief. Yet once again he worked a miracle for them, changing that sheer rock into flowing water. When the slavish pleasure of food once more stirred up their gluttonous desire, and, though they lacked none of the necessities of life, they dreamed of the plenty of Egypt, they were disciplined with harsher whips, like unruly youths: serpents throughout the camp struck them and injected deadly venom with their bite. As death followed death from these creatures, the lawgiver, moved by divine counsel, cast bronze in the likeness of a serpent and set it on a height so that it could be seen above the whole camp. In this way he stopped the destruction the creatures were causing among the people. For whoever looked at the image of the serpent in bronze had nothing to fear from the bite of the real serpent, since the sight blunted the venom by some secret counteracting power. Again there was an uprising from among the people against his leadership, and some tried by force to take the priesthood for themselves. He became a suppliant to God for the sinners, but the justice of God's judgment was stronger than Moses' compassion for his own people. For by God's will the earth split open in a chasm and closed again, swallowing up with their whole households all who had risen against Moses' rule. Those who had raged after the priesthood, about two hundred and fifty of them, were consumed by fire, and by their own fate they taught their kinsmen restraint. To persuade men all the more that the grace of the priesthood comes from God to those he judges worthy, rods are brought from the leading men of each tribe, each giver having marked his own with letters, and among them was that of Aaron the priest. He placed these in the sanctuary and through them revealed to the people God's verdict on the priesthood. For of them all, only Aaron's rod budded, and it brought forth fruit from the wood and ripened it (the fruit was a nut). This seemed a very great wonder even to the unbelievers: how a piece of wood without bark, scraped smooth, and

without roots, suddenly grew vigorous and did what rooted plants do, since divine power took the place of earth, bark, moisture, root and branches for the wood. After this, leading his army through foreign nations, he gave his sworn word that he would not let the people pass through their fields and vineyards, but would keep to the royal road, turning aside neither to the right nor to the left. When the enemy would not make peace even on these terms, he defeated his adversary in battle and won control of the passage. Then a certain Balak, who ruled over a larger nation (the nation was called the Midianites), was struck with dismay at the fate of those who had already perished, and expected that he would very soon suffer the same at the hands of the Israelites. So he brought in as an ally no help of weapons or men, but curious sorcery, through a certain Balaam. Balaam claimed to be skilled in such things, and those who had employed him believed that he had some power for such undertakings. His art was augury, but with the cooperation of demons he was dangerous, bringing incurable harms upon people by a more occult power. As he followed those who were taking him to the king of that nation, he was taught by the voice of his donkey that the journey would not turn out well for him. Then, having learned through an apparition what he was to do, he found his malicious sorcery too weak to inflict any harm on those whom God was fighting for. Instead of being moved by the working of demons, he became inspired by divine breath, and he uttered such words as were plainly a prophecy of things that would later turn out for the better. For through the very things by which his art was prevented from working evil, he came to perceive the divine power; he bade farewell to divination and became the spokesman of the divine will. After this the foreign nation was crushed, since the people prevailed in the war. But afterward the people were defeated by the passion of licentiousness with the captive women, until Phinehas pierced through with a single blow those who were joined in disgrace, and God's wrath against those who had run mad after lawless unions came to an end. Then the lawgiver climbed a high mountain and surveyed from afar the land that had been prepared for Israel through the divine promise made to the fathers, and he departed from human life, leaving on earth no sign and no memorial of his departure in a tomb. Time did not harm his beauty: it did not dim the brightness of his eyes or dull the radiant grace of his face. He remained always the same, and within mutable nature he kept his beauty unchanging. These, then, are the things we have learned from the plain history of the man, and we have told them in brief, even though in places the subject necessarily drew the account out. It is now time to apply the life we have recalled to the purpose set before us in this discourse, so that what has been said may make some contribution to the life of virtue. Let us, then, go back to the beginning of the story about him.

CONTEMPLATION ON THE LIFE OF MOSES. Moses was born at the time when the tyrant's law ordered that male children be destroyed. How then shall we imitate by our own choice this man's birth, which happened by chance? Someone will surely say that this is not in our power, so that a person could imitate that celebrated birth in his own birth. But there is nothing wrong with beginning the imitation from what seems most difficult. For who does not know that everything subject to change never remains the same as itself, but is always coming to be one thing from another, with change always at work toward either the better or the worse? Let this be understood figuratively. The material and passionate disposition, toward which human nature slides and is carried, is the female offspring of life, whose birth pleases the tyrant. But the austere and vigorous quality of virtue is the male child, hostile to the tyrant and suspected of rising up against his rule. Whatever is subject to change must, then, always be in some way coming to birth. For in mutable nature nothing can be observed that always remains the same. Yet being born in this way does not come from an outside impulse, as happens with those who beget bodily whatever chance brings. Such a birth comes about by choice. And we are in a sense our own fathers, giving birth to ourselves as we wish, and by our own choice shaping ourselves into whatever form we want, male or female, according to the principle of virtue or of vice. It is certainly possible for us, even if the tyrant is unwilling and grieved, to come into the light by the better birth, to be seen with pleasure by the parents of this fair offspring (these would be the reasonings that become fathers of virtue), and to be kept alive, even against the tyrant's will. Therefore, if one may take the starting points from the history and uncover the riddle more plainly, the text teaches this: the beginning of the virtuous life is to be born to the enemy's grief, in that kind of birth, I mean, whose labor is brought to delivery by choice. For no one could grieve the adversary without showing in himself such marks as become proofs of his victory over him. It belongs entirely to the same choice both to beget this manly and courageous offspring, to nurse it with the proper nourishment, and to take care that it may be saved from the water unharmed. For those who make their offspring a gift to the tyrant hand their children over to the stream naked and uncared for. By the stream I mean life, which is tossed by the waves of passion after passion; by it

whatever falls into the stream is dragged under and drowned. But prudent and provident reasonings, the fathers of the manly offspring, when the necessity of life compels them to expose their good child to the waves of life, secure him in an ark, so that the one given over to the stream will not sink to the bottom. The ark, made of various boards fitted together, would be education, which is put together from various branches of learning and holds above the waves of life the one who is carried along in it. With it, he will not wander long on the tossing waters, borne along by the rush of the waves. Rather, he will reach the firm ground of the bank, that is, he will come to be outside the turmoil of life, pushed of his own accord by the current toward solid land. This we learn by experience too: the unstable and drifting movement of affairs itself pushes away those who are no longer plunged along with it in human deceits, regarding them as a useless burden because by their virtue they trouble it. Let the one who has come out of these things imitate Moses and not spare his tears, even if he happens to be secured in an ark. For tears are a sure guardian of those who are saved through virtue. The barren and sterile daughter of the king (who, I think, is properly to be understood as pagan philosophy) adopts the youth and wishes to be called his mother. The text permits us not to reject this kinship with a falsely named mother so long as one sees in oneself the immaturity of youth. But once he has grown up, as we learned about Moses, he will consider it shameful to be called the son of one who is barren by nature. For pagan education is truly barren: it is always in labor and never brings its child to life. For what fruit worthy of so many and such great pains has philosophy shown for its long travail? Are not all its offspring like wind-eggs, never brought to term, miscarried before they come into the light of the knowledge of God, though they could have become men if [?]... Having lived [with her] only so long as not to seem to have no share in what they hold in honor, let him run back to his natural mother, from whom he was not separated even while being raised by the princess, since he was nursed, as the history says, with his mother's milk. This seems to me to teach that, if we engage with pagan learning during the time of our education, we should not separate ourselves from the milk of the Church that nourishes us. This would be the laws and customs of the Church, by which the soul is nourished and grows strong, receiving from them the starting points for its ascent to the heights. True is the saying that whoever looks to pagan doctrines rather than to those of his fathers will find himself between two enemies. For the one who is a foreigner in religion opposes the Hebrew teaching, striving to show himself stronger than the Israelite. And to many of the more superficial he has seemed so; they abandoned their ancestral faith, fought on the side of the enemy, and became transgressors of the teaching of their fathers. But the one who, like Moses, is great and noble in soul strikes down and kills the one who rises up against the teaching of true religion. One could find such a battle in us as well. For man is set in the middle like a prize in a contest for those who contend for him from opposite sides, and to whichever

he joins himself, he makes that one victor over the other: for instance, idolatry and godliness, licentiousness and self-control, justice and injustice, pride and humility, and all things that are understood as opposites. This is plainly the battle of an Egyptian against a Hebrew. Moses, then, teaches us by his own example to stand by virtue as by a kinsman, and to slay whatever attacks virtue from the opposite side. For in truth the victory of true religion becomes the death and destruction of idolatry. So too injustice is killed by justice, and pride is slain by humility. But a strife among kinsmen against one another also takes place within us. For the doctrine-making of wicked heresies would never have found room unless reasonings had ranged themselves in opposing ranks against those that are truer. If, then, we are too weak to give the victory to what is right by our own strength, because the worse side prevails through its arguments and pushes away the very principle of truth, we must flee from there as quickly as possible, following the example of the history, to the greater and loftier teaching of the mysteries. And if we must once more associate with a foreigner, that is, if need compels us to associate with pagan philosophy, let us choose this too, after first driving the wicked shepherds away from their unjust use of the wells; that is, after refuting the teachers of evil for their wicked use of learning. Then we will live apart by ourselves, no longer entangled with combatants or caught between them. Instead we will live among those of one mind and one judgment, whom we ourselves pasture, all the movements of our soul being shepherded like sheep by the will of reason that presides over them. And so, as we persevere in this peaceful and unwarlike way of life, the truth will then shine upon us, illuminating the eyes of the soul with its own rays. And the truth is God, who then appeared to Moses through that ineffable illumination. If the light that illuminated the prophet's soul was kindled from a thorny bush, this too will not be without value for our inquiry. For if God is truth, and truth is light (and the voice of the Gospel bears witness to these lofty and divine names for the God who appeared to us in the flesh), it follows that such a [?] of virtue

[?] to run up to that height where the light of truth is seen, unless the dead and earthly covering of skins is loosed from the feet of the soul, the covering that was put around our nature in the beginning, when we were stripped naked through disobedience to the divine will. And when this has been done, the knowledge of the truth will follow for us; [?] it becomes a purification from our false notion about what does not exist. This, at least in my account, is the definition of truth: not to be deceived in our apprehension of what exists. (For falsehood is an impression about what does not exist, arising in the mind as though what has no being had real existence; but truth is the secure apprehension of what exists.) And so, having devoted himself in quiet over a long period to lofty studies, a person will barely come to understand what truly being is, which has its existence by its own nature, and what non-being is, which exists only in appearance, having in itself a nature without substance. This, it seems to me, is what the great Moses then learned when he was taught in the theophany: that none of the other things, whether those grasped by the senses or those contemplated by the mind, really subsists, except the essence that stands above all and is the cause of the universe, on which everything depends. For even if the mind sees something else among the things that exist, reason does not perceive in any of them the self-sufficiency by which it could exist without participating in Being. But that which is always the same, neither increasing nor diminishing, equally unmoved by every change, whether for the better or for the worse (for it is far removed from the worse, and there is nothing better than it), needing nothing else, alone desirable, participated in by all, and not diminished when those who partake of it share in it: this is truly that which really is, and the apprehension of it is the knowledge of the truth. So then, coming to this, he at that time, and now everyone who, like him, loosens the earthly covering from himself and looks to the light from the bush, that is, to the ray that shone upon us through this thorny flesh, which is, as the Gospel says, the true light and the truth, then becomes such a one as is able to bring salvation to others as well: to overthrow the tyranny that wickedly prevails, and to deliver into freedom all who are held fast in evil slavery, with the transformed right hand and the staff turned into a serpent leading the way in the miracles. By these, it seems to me, the mystery of the Lord's coming in the flesh is figuratively indicated, the Godhead that appeared to men, through which both the overthrow of the tyrant and the freedom of those held in his power come about. What leads me to this interpretation is the testimony of prophecy and the Gospel. For the Prophet says, "This is the change of the right hand of the Most High," since the divine nature, though contemplated as unchangeable, yet by condescending to the weakness of human nature, to our shape and form

was changed. For there too the lawgiver's hand, when brought out of his bosom, was changed to an unnatural color, and when it was put back into his bosom, it returned to its own natural grace. And the only-begotten God, who is in the bosom of the Father, is himself the right hand of the Most High. When he appeared to us from the bosom, he was changed to be like us. But when, having wiped away our infirmities, he brought back to his own bosom the hand that had been among us and had taken on our color (and the Father is the bosom of the right hand), he did not change the impassible nature into passibility, but transformed the mutable and passible into impassibility through its communion with the immutable. Let not the change of the staff into a serpent trouble those who love Christ, as though we were fitting the meaning of the mystery to an unseemly animal. For the Truth himself, through the voice of the Gospel, does not refuse such an image, when he says, "For just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up." And the meaning is clear. For if the father of sin is called a serpent by divine Scripture, then what is born of the serpent is surely a serpent too. It follows that sin bears the same name as the one who begot it. Yet the apostolic word testifies that the Lord became sin for our sake, [?] our sinful [nature]; [?] the figure is fitted to the Lord. For if sin is a serpent and the Lord became sin, [?] he, who is nothing other than sin [?], for our sake becomes a serpent, in order to devour and consume the Egyptian serpents brought to life by the sorcerers. When this has been done, he changes back into the staff, by which sinners are disciplined, while those who are climbing the steep and hard road of virtue find rest, leaning through good hopes on the staff of faith. "For faith is the substance of things hoped for." Whoever has come to understand these things becomes plainly a god to those who resist the truth and are infatuated with this material and insubstantial deception, people for whom hearing about the One who is is despised as something worthless. For Pharaoh says, "Who is he, that I should listen to his voice? I do not know the Lord." To those who live by the more irrational senses, only what is material and fleshly is thought valuable. If, then, a person is so strengthened by the shining of the light, and gains such strength and authority against his opponents, then, like an athlete who has thoroughly trained in athletic courage under a trainer, he now strips for the contest against his enemies with confidence and assurance, holding in his hand that staff, that is, the word of faith, by which he is to overcome the Egyptian serpents. And his foreign wife will follow him too; for there is something in pagan education that is not to be rejected for union with us in begetting virtue. For indeed ethical

…and natural philosophy might at some time become the spouse, friend and life-partner of the higher life, provided only that her offspring bring with them nothing of the foreign defilement. For unless this is circumcised and cut away, so that everything harmful and unclean is removed, the angel who meets him brings the fear of death. His wife appeases the angel by showing her offspring to be pure, through the removal of the mark by which the foreigner is recognized. I think that for anyone initiated into the historical narrative, what has been said makes plain the sequence of progress in virtue that the account points to, as it follows in due order the chain of the historical riddles. For in the offspring that philosophy begets through secular learning there is something fleshly and uncircumcised; when this is cut away, what remains belongs to the nobility of Israel. For example, the outside philosophy also says that the soul is immortal. This is the pious offspring. But that the soul passes from body to body and is changed from a rational nature into an irrational one: this is the fleshly and foreign foreskin. And there are many other such things. It says that God exists, but it thinks of him as material. It confesses him to be Creator, but as needing matter in order to create. It grants that he is good and powerful, but holds that in many things he gives way to the necessity of fate. Why should one go through the details one by one, showing how the good doctrines of the outside philosophy are defiled by absurd additions? When these are cut away, the angel of God becomes gracious to us, rejoicing as over the genuine offspring of such doctrines. But we must return to the sequence of our discourse, so that the alliance of a brother may one day come to meet us too as we draw near to the contests in Egypt. For we have learned that at the beginning of his life of virtue Moses had encounters that were warlike and contentious: an Egyptian was oppressing a Hebrew, and again a Hebrew was quarreling with his fellow countryman. But once he had been raised to the greater achievements of the soul, through long diligence and through the illumination that came to him on the height, the encounter is friendly and peaceful, for his brother was moved by God to come and meet him. If what happened in history is transferred to a more figurative contemplation, nothing in it will be found useless for our purpose. For in truth, those who succeed in virtue are also joined by the alliance that God gave to our nature. This alliance is older, dating from our first birth, but it is revealed and recognized only when, having made ourselves sufficiently at home in the higher life through attention and diligence, we strip for the harder contests. So that we do not explain riddles by riddles, I will set out the meaning of this more plainly. There is an account, trustworthy because it comes from the tradition of the fathers, which says this. When our nature fell into sin, God did not neglect our fall and leave it without his providence. Instead he appointed an angel, one of those whose lot is an incorporeal nature, to stand by each person's life as an ally. On the opposite side, the destroyer of our nature devised a counterpart: an evil and harmful

demon, who does injury to human life. Man stands between the two, and each of his companions has an aim opposed to the other's. By his own choice he makes the one prevail over the other. The good angel sets before his reason the goods of virtue, which those who succeed see through hope. The other sets before him material pleasures, which hold out no hope of good, but which enslave the senses of the more foolish because they are present, enjoyed and seen. If, then, someone withdraws from those that lure him to evil and turns his reason toward the better, he has, as it were, put vice behind his back. He sets his own soul face to face with the hope of good things, like a mirror, so as to imprint on the purity of his soul the images and reflections of the virtue that God shows him. Then the alliance of his brother comes to meet him and stands with him. For the angel is in a way a brother to the rational and intelligent part of the human soul. As has been said, he appears and stands beside us at the moment when we draw near to Pharaoh. Someone may think that the exposition of the history has been set entirely alongside the sequence of this contemplation of the mind. If somewhere he finds something written that falls outside this meaning, let him not reject the whole because of it. Let him always remember the aim of our discourse, which we keep in view as we go through these things. We said at the very beginning that the lives of distinguished men are set before those who come after as a pattern of virtue. Those who emulate them cannot go through the very material of those events. For how could there again be a people multiplying in Egypt after migrating there? Or again an enslaving tyrant, hostile to male offspring and increasing the softer and weaker to a multitude, along with everything else the account contains? Since, then, it has been shown impossible to imitate the wonders of the blessed in the events themselves, we must transfer whatever can be applied from the material sequence to some moral teaching. In this way those who are eager for virtue may find help toward such a life. And if, among the events of the history, something was forced by the necessity of the events to fall outside the sequence of the elevated meaning, let us pass over it as unprofitable and useless for our purpose. Let us not break off the guidance toward virtue where we are able to keep it. I say this about what has been understood concerning Aaron, to remedy in advance the objection that follows. For someone will say that he does not dispute that the angel is akin to the soul in being intelligible and incorporeal, that it existed before our formation, and that it stands with those who grapple with their adversaries. But, he will say, it is not right to take Aaron, who led the Israelites into idolatry, as a type of that angel. To him we shall reply, setting the sequence aside for a moment, with what we have already said: what lies outside our aim should not overturn the harmony of the rest. We shall also say that

"brother" and "angel" are both terms with more than one meaning, and each may perhaps be applied with opposite meanings. For there is said to be an angel not only of God but also of Satan, and we call not only the good man but also the wicked one a brother. Thus Scripture says of the better sort: "Let brothers be useful in times of need," and of the opposite sort: "Every brother will trip you with his heel." Having set these points beside the sequence of our discourse, and having deferred a more exact contemplation of them to their proper place, let us now take up the matter before us. He, then, had strengthened himself by the light that appeared to him and had gained such a brother as ally and helper. Now he boldly addresses words on behalf of the truth to the people, reminds them of their ancestral nobility, and gives them counsel on how they might escape the misery of clay and brick. What, then, does the history teach us through these things? That anyone who has not prepared his speech through such training should not venture to address the multitude. You see how, when he was still young, before he had grown so far in virtue, he was not thought a credible counsellor of peace even to two men who were quarrelling. Yet now he speaks to so many thousands at once. The history all but cries out to you: do not venture to teach and counsel your hearers unless you have perfected your ability for it through diligence of this kind and degree. But when the better words have been spoken, freedom has been pointed out, and the hearers have been strengthened in their desire for it, the enemy is provoked and makes the suffering of those who obey the word worse. This too is not foreign to what happens now. For many who have received the word that sets them free from tyranny, and have attached themselves to the preaching, are still harassed by the adversary with the assaults of temptations. Through these many become more approved and firmer in the faith, hardened like steel by the onset of afflictions. But some of the weaker ones even give way under such misfortunes. They say openly that it would have been better for them to remain without hearing the preaching of freedom than to meet with such things because of it. This also happened then, when the Israelites in their faintheartedness blamed those who had announced their release from slavery. But the word will not stop drawing us toward the good, even if someone still infant and immature in mind shrinks back like a child from temptations he is not used to. For this was what the harmful and destructive demon was eager to bring about against men: that his subject should not look up to heaven but stoop toward the earth and make bricks out of the clay within himself. For whatever belongs to material enjoyment certainly comes from earth or water, as is plain to everyone

[?] cities, among those divided between opposing opinions, for some the stream of faith that they draw through divine teaching is drinkable and clear. But for those who play the Egyptian through wicked assumptions, the water becomes the blood of corruption. And often the sophistry of deception tries to turn even the drink of the Hebrews into blood through the defilement of falsehood. That is, it tries to show our teaching, even to us, as other than it is. Yet it could never make the drink wholly useless, even if by deceit it reddens its surface appearance. For the Hebrew drinks the true water, even if it is plausibly slandered by his opponents, and pays no attention to the appearance the deception gives it. So too the race of frogs, ugly and noisy, whose life is amphibious and whose leap is a kind of crawling, and unpleasant not only in appearance but also in [?] of the skin [?]

How, then, could he be [?], if by necessity from above he was disposed harshly and resistantly? And somewhere the divine Apostle says the same, that since they did not see fit to have God in

to everyone. This covers whatever is pursued for the belly and for feasting, and whatever is done for the sake of wealth. The mixture of these elements becomes clay and is called clay. Those who gape after clay-like pleasures fill themselves with it, yet they never keep full the space that receives the pleasures. What is always being filled becomes empty again for whatever flows in next. For so the brickmaker [?]; anyone who looks now at one disposition, now at another, would easily understand the riddle. For whoever has filled his desire with one of the things he pursued, if his desire then turns toward something else, finds himself empty again for that. And if he becomes full of this, he is again empty and has room for yet another. This never ceases working in us at every moment, until a person escapes from the material life. Then there is the stalk, and the chaff that comes from it, which the one who obeys tyrannical commands is forced to mix into the brick. Both the divine Gospel and the lofty voice of the Apostle alike interpret both the chaff and the stalk as fuel for the fire. So whenever one of those eminent in virtue wishes to draw those enslaved to deception toward a philosophical and free life, the one who, as the Apostle says, plays the sophist against our souls with various wiles knows how to set the sophistries of deception against the divine law. I say this with the Egyptian serpents in view, that is, the various vices of deception. The rod of Moses brings about their destruction, and we have already contemplated what is fitting about it in moderate measure. He, then, who possesses that invincible rod of virtue, which destroys the rods made by sophistry, advances by a certain path and order to the greater wonders. This wonder-working does not aim to astonish those who meet with it; it looks to the benefit of those who are being saved. For by the same wonders of virtue the enemy is destroyed and the kindred people increased. Let us first learn the most general aim of the guidance given through the particular wonders. Then it will be possible for us to apply the meaning to each one. For the teaching of the truth changes along with the dispositions of those who receive the word. The word shows evil or good to everyone equally. The one who readily obeys what is shown has his mind in the light. But for the one who is resistant and refuses to open his soul to look toward the ray of truth, the darkness of ignorance remains. If what we have understood in general about such things is not false, then the particulars cannot be otherwise either, since examining the parts one by one is proved together with the general argument. So it is nothing remarkable that the Hebrew remains untouched by the plagues of Egypt while living among the foreigners, since even now one can see the same thing happening. For among those in [?] cities

that are at odds within themselves, among those divided between opposing opinions, for some the stream of faith that they draw through divine teaching is drinkable and clear. But for those who play the Egyptian through wicked assumptions, the water becomes the blood of corruption. And often the sophistry of deception tries to turn even the drink of the Hebrews into blood through the defilement of falsehood. That is, it tries to show our teaching, even to us, as other than it is. Yet it could never make the drink wholly useless, even if by deceit it reddens its surface appearance. For the Hebrew drinks the true water, even if it is plausibly slandered by his opponents, and pays no attention to the appearance the deception gives it. So too with the race of frogs, ugly and noisy, whose life is amphibious and whose leap is a kind of crawling (unpleasant not only in appearance but also in the foul smell of its skin). It creeps into the houses, the beds and the storerooms of the Egyptians, but it does not touch the life of the Hebrews. For in truth the destructive offspring of vice are plainly races of frogs, brought to life out of the filthy human heart as if out of mire. These frogs live in the houses of those who play the Egyptian in the way of life they have chosen. They appear even on the tables, they do not keep away from the beds, and they slip into the storerooms where things are put away. Look at the filthy and licentious life, which is truly born of clay and mire. By imitating the irrational, it does not remain exactly in either nature in its manner of living. Such a man is human by nature but becomes a beast through passion, and so he displays that amphibious and double form of life. In him you will find the marks of this disease not only on the bed but also on the table, in the storerooms, and throughout the whole dwelling. For such a person shows his profligacy in everything, so that from what is pursued in the house anyone can easily recognize the life of the licentious man and of the pure one. In the one house, on the plaster of the walls, art displays images that kindle passionate pleasure. Through them nature is reminded of its disease, as passion pours into the soul through the eyes from those shameful sights. In the house of the temperate man, every precaution and forethought is taken so that the eye, too, may be kept pure of passionate sights. Likewise the table of the temperate man is pure, while the table of one who wallows in the miry life is found froglike and heavy with meat. And if you search the storerooms, that is, the hidden and secret parts of his life, you will observe a far greater heap of frogs among the licentious. If the history says that the rod of virtue does these things against the Egyptians, let us not be troubled by the account. For the history also says that the tyrant was hardened by God. How, then, could he be condemned, if he was disposed harshly and resistantly by a necessity from above? And somewhere the divine Apostle says the same: that since they did not see fit to have God in

their knowledge, God gave them up to dishonorable passions. He is speaking of men who corrupt males and of those who disgrace themselves in the dishonorable and unspeakable forms of profligacy. But even if divine Scripture speaks in this way, God does not hand over to the passion of dishonor the one who is carried toward it. Nor is Pharaoh hardened by the divine will, nor is the froglike life fashioned by virtue. For if this were the will of the divine nature, such a choice would certainly have prevailed in everyone equally, so that no difference of virtue and vice would be seen in human life. But people take part in life in different ways: some succeed through virtue, while others slide into vice. So one could not reasonably attribute the differences between lives to some overruling necessities established by the divine will, since in each case free choice holds the power. Who, then, is handed over to the passion of dishonor? We can learn this clearly from the Apostle: the one who did not see fit to have God in his knowledge. God does not hand him over to passion in retaliation for not being acknowledged by him as God. Rather, his failure to know God becomes the cause of his being dragged down into the passionate and dishonorable life. Suppose someone said that the sun, by not being seen, threw so-and-so into a pit. We would not think that the luminary grew angry and pushed into the pit the man who refused to look at it. The saying would reasonably be understood to mean that not sharing in the light is what caused the man who does not see to fall into the pit. In the same way it is reverent to understand the Apostle's words, that those who did not acknowledge God are given over to dishonorable passions. So too with the statement that the Egyptian tyrant was hardened by God. It does not mean that the divine will placed the resistance in Pharaoh's soul. It means that his free choice, by inclining toward vice, would not receive the word that softens resistance. So too the rod of virtue, when it appears among the Egyptians, makes the Hebrew pure of the froglike life but shows the Egyptian life to be full of this disease. Yet sometimes, when Moses stretches out his hands on their behalf as well, the frogs are destroyed. One can see this happening now too. Consider those who have perceived the stretching out of the lawgiver's hands. (You will surely understand that the riddle is speaking to you: by the lawgiver you are to understand the true Lawgiver, and by the stretching out of the hands, him who stretched out his hands on the cross.) Those, then, who for a while live with these filthy and froglike thoughts, if they look to him who stretched out his hands for us, are freed from their evil cohabitation, as the passion is put to death and rots away. For truly, to those who have been freed from this disease,

…after the deadening of those creeping movements, the memory of one's former life becomes something [?] and foul-smelling, sickening the soul with shame. As the Apostle says to those who have turned from evil to pursue virtue: "What fruit, then, did you have at that time from the things of which you are now ashamed?" In the same sense, please understand the air as well, which through the rod was darkened for the eyes of the Egyptians but lit up by the sun for the Hebrews. This above all confirms the interpretation already given: no compelling power from above causes one person to be in darkness and another in light. We human beings have within ourselves, in our own nature and choice, the causes of both light and darkness, and we become whichever of the two we wish. For according to the history, it was not some wall or mountain blocking their sight and shutting out the rays that let the Hebrews revel in the light while the others had no perception of the gift. In the same way, although the life of light lies equally before everyone and within their power, some walk in darkness, driven by wicked practices into the gloom of vice, while others are made radiant by the light of virtue. And if, after three days of suffering in darkness, the Egyptians too come to share in the light, someone might perhaps start from this and apply the meaning to the change from vice to virtue of those who once lived like Egyptians, a change that comes through knowledge of the Crucified One and through repentance. For that darkness which could be felt, as the history calls it, is closely related, both in word and in meaning, to the darkness of ignorance and sin. Each of these is dispelled when Moses stretches out his hands on behalf of those in darkness, as was explained earlier. Likewise that furnace soot, which brought painful boils upon the Egyptians, might reasonably be understood, through the riddle in the word "furnace", as the punishment by fire threatened in Gehenna. It touches only those who live like Egyptians, that is, as we have often said, those who live wickedly and do not worship the outstretched hands of Christ. But if someone is truly an Israelite and a son of Abraham, and looks to him in the way he lives, so as to show by his choice his kinship with the race of the elect, he is kept safe from the pain of that furnace. And perhaps for the others too, the interpretation given of Moses' outstretched hands may one day become a cure for their pain and a release from their punishments.
