As for those tiny gnats that torment the Egyptians with their unseen bites, the dog-fly that fastens painfully on bodies with its bite, the crops ruined by the locusts, and the fiery whirlwinds from above falling together with the hailstones: anyone who follows the line of what has already been examined would have no trouble fitting each of these to the corresponding meanings. All of them are produced in the first place by the Egyptian choice, and brought upon it by the impartial justice of God. Following this through, let us understand that it is [not] from God that painful things come to those who deserve them, but that each person becomes the maker of his own plagues, preparing the store of suffering through his

own choice. As the Apostle says to such a person: "By your hardness and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God, who will repay each one according to his works." Think of a rather disorderly diet, which produces some harmful, bilious humor in the bowels. When the physician uses his skill to draw it out by vomiting, no one would blame him for putting the diseased humor into the body. The disorderly eating produced it; medical science only brought it into the open. In the same way, even if the painful retribution that falls on those whose choice is wicked is said to come from God, it is reasonable to understand that such sufferings take their beginnings and causes from ourselves. For the one who has lived without sin there is no darkness, no worm, no Gehenna, no fire, nor any other of those fearful names and things, just as the history says that the Egyptian plagues did not touch the Hebrews. If, then, in the same place a thing is evil for one person and not for another, and the difference in their choices shows which applies to each, it is clear that none of these evils can exist apart from our own choice. But let us go on to what follows in the account, having learned this much from what we have examined. When Moses, and whoever raises himself up by virtue as he did, has been strengthened in soul by long attention to the upright and lofty life and by the illumination that comes from above, he considers it a loss not to lead his kinsmen as well to the life of freedom. Going to them, he sets before them the harsher sufferings they endure, and so instills in them a stronger longing for freedom. And when he is about to rescue his people from evil, he brings death upon every Egyptian firstborn. By what he did he lays down a law for us: we must destroy evil at its first birth, for there is no other way to escape the Egyptian life. It seems right to me not to pass over this idea without examining it. If one looks only at the history, how can a notion worthy of God be kept in the events said to have happened? The Egyptian does wrong, and in his place his newborn infant is punished, who because of his age cannot yet tell good from bad. His life lies outside the passion of vice. Infancy has no room for passion. It does not know the difference between right and left. It looks only to the breast. Its one sign that something hurts is tears, and if it gets something its nature desires, it shows its pleasure with a smile. And this child pays the penalty for his father's wickedness! Where is justice? Where is piety? Where is holiness? Where is Ezekiel, who cries out, "The soul that sins, it shall die," and "The son shall not bear the sin of the father"? How can the history legislate against that word? Would it not be more reasonable, then, to look to the higher meaning and believe that, even if something happened figuratively, the lawgiver is setting forth a teaching through the

events? The teaching is this: whoever grapples with vice by means of virtue must destroy the first beginnings of evils. For when the beginning is destroyed, what comes after it vanishes along with it. The Lord teaches this in the Gospel, almost crying aloud that we should destroy the firstborn of the Egyptian evils, when he commands us to do away with desire and anger and so no longer fear either the stain of adultery or the guilt of murder. Neither of these could come into being by itself unless anger brought murder to completion, and desire adultery. Since, then, the one who breeds for vice gives birth to desire before adultery and to anger before murder, whoever destroys the firstborn certainly destroys with it the brood that follows the firstborn. In the same way, whoever strikes a snake's head kills along with it the whole coil it drags behind. But this could not happen unless that blood which turns the destroyer away had been poured on our entrances. If we should examine the interpretation given more precisely in what has been said, the history lets us understand this through both things: the killing of the firstborn and the securing of the entrance with blood. In the first, the first impulse of evil is destroyed. In the second, the first entrance of vice against us is turned back through the true Lamb. For we do not use some device to drive out the destroyer once he is inside. Rather, we set up a guard through the law so that he cannot slip in at all. The guard and the safeguard is to mark the lintel and the doorposts of the entrance with the blood of the lamb. Here the word is teaching us in riddles about the nature of the soul, something that secular learning also grasped when it divided the soul into the rational, the appetitive, and the spirited parts. Of these, they say, desire [and spirit?] are placed below, supporting the thinking part of the soul from either side, while reason is yoked to both, holding them together and being held up by them: it is sharpened to courage by spirit and lifted up to share in the good through desire. As long as the soul stays secured in this arrangement, made firm by virtuous thoughts as if by bolts, all its parts work together with one another toward the good. Reason by its own power gives security to the parts beneath it and in turn receives the same favor from them. But if the arrangement is turned upside down and the upper becomes lower, so that reason falls to the trodden-down part and places the appetitive and spirited disposition above itself, then the destroyer slips inside. Nothing from the blood stands against him to block his entrance; that is, faith in Christ does not fight alongside people in that condition. For he commands that the blood be smeared first on the upper lintel, and only then that it touch the doorposts on either side. How, then, could anyone smear the upper part first, when it is not found

above? And if these two things, the killing of the firstborn and the pouring of the blood, did not both happen to the Israelites, do not be surprised. Do not reject for that reason the interpretation given about the destruction of evil, as if it had been invented apart from the truth. Here we have understood the difference between the names "Israelite" and "Egyptian" as the difference between virtue and vice. If, then, the higher sense invites us to understand the virtuous person as the Israelite, it would be unreasonable to look for the first offspring of virtue to be slaughtered. It is rather those offspring that are better destroyed than raised. So it follows that God has taught us that the first offspring of the Egyptian brood must be destroyed, so that evil may die out, consumed along with the destruction of its beginning. And the history agrees with this meaning. The Israelite offspring are protected by the pouring of the blood, so that the good may come to maturity. But whatever would add to the Egyptian people once it matured was destroyed before it could mature in evil. What comes next, taken together with the interpretation of the account, also supports the higher sense we have proposed. For he wants the body from which the blood flowed to become our food, the blood that, displayed on the entrances, keeps away the destroyer of the Egyptians. And he wants the posture of those who eat this food to be tense and hurried, not like what one sees among those enjoying themselves at banquets, whose hands are relaxed, whose clothes hang loosely, and whose feet are free of anything for the road. Everything is the opposite. Their feet are bound in sandals, a belt cinches the flowing tunic at the waist, and in their hand is the staff for fending off dogs. In this posture the food is set before them without any cook's seasoning, thrown together on the fire from whatever was at hand. The diners devour it greedily in all haste, until the whole body of the animal has been eaten. They gnaw around the bones for whatever is edible but do not touch what is inside, for breaking the bones of this animal is forbidden. Whatever is left of the meal is consumed by fire. From all this it is clear that the letter points to some higher meaning.

…life, driven by necessity itself to depart from the moment we are born. For this departure we must be prepared in our hands and feet and with whatever else makes the road safe. So that we may not be hurt by the thorns of this life (and the thorns are our sins) by walking with bare and unprotected feet, let us protect our feet with sturdy sandals. These are the self-controlled and austere life, which by its own strength breaks and snaps off the points of the thorns, and keeps sin from slipping inside from some small, unnoticed beginning. A tunic that billows around the feet and hangs down to them would hinder anyone running this road in haste. Following this line, we may understand the tunic as the broad enjoyment of the things people strive for in this life, which temperate reasoning draws in tight when it becomes the traveler's belt. That the belt is temperance is shown by the place where it is fastened [?]. The staff that wards off wild beasts is the word of hope, with which we support whatever in the soul is flagging and drive off whatever barks at us. The food set before us from the fire is, I say, this warm and fiery faith, which we accept without delay. We eat as much of it as the eater can readily take, but what lies hidden in the harder and tougher thoughts, and in the word, we leave unexplored and unpried into, handing such food over to the fire. To make these riddles clear, we say this: those divine precepts that are easy to understand should be pursued neither sluggishly nor under compulsion. Rather, like hungry people, we should eagerly fill ourselves with what is set before us, so that the food may give us strength for good health. But as for the meanings that are hidden, such as asking what the essence of God is, what existed before creation, what lies beyond the visible world, what the necessity behind events is, and all the other questions that curious people investigate, these we should leave to the Holy Spirit alone to know, who searches the depths of God, as the Apostle says. No one educated in Scripture is unaware that Scripture often mentions and names fire in place of the Spirit. The precept of Wisdom also leads us to this meaning: "Do not search into things too strong for you," that is, do not break the bones of the word, "for you have no need of hidden things." This is how Moses leads the people out of Egypt. And everyone who follows in Moses' footsteps in this way [?] frees from the Egyptian tyranny all those whom the word guides. But I think those who

follow the one who leads them toward virtue must not be poor in Egyptian wealth or lacking in the treasures of the foreigners. They should take everything that belongs to their opponents and keep it for their own use, which is what Moses then commanded the people to do. If we take this in its obvious sense, we cannot accept the lawgiver's intention, since he would be ordering the people to cheat those who lent to them, and would be teaching injustice. Nor could anyone truly say that the lawgiver orders such things, if he looks at the laws that follow, which everywhere forbid wronging one's neighbor. Some may think it reasonable that by this device the Israelites collected their wages from the Egyptians. But the charge is no lighter, since such a command is not free of lying and deceit. Whoever takes something on loan and does not give it back to the lender has done wrong by defrauding him, if the thing belongs to someone else. If it is his own and he keeps it, he has tricked the person who lent in the hope of getting it back, and he is called a cheat in any case. So the higher sense is more fitting than the obvious meaning. It commands those who pursue the life of freedom through virtue to supply themselves also with the wealth of outside learning, in which those who are foreign to the faith take pride. Moral and natural philosophy, geometry and astronomy, logic, and everything studied by those outside the Church: the leader in virtue commands us to take these from those in Egypt who are rich in such things and to receive them on loan, since they will be useful in due time, when the divine temple of the mystery must be adorned with the riches of reason. For those who have stored up such wealth for themselves bring it to Moses as he labors over the tent of testimony, each contributing his own share to the furnishing of the holy place. We can see this happening even now. Many people bring outside learning as a kind of gift to the Church of God. Such was the great Basil, who in his youth traded well with the wealth of Egypt, dedicated it to God, and with that wealth adorned the true tent of the Church. But we must return to where we left off. Those who are already looking toward virtue and following the lawgiver in their lives, once they leave the borders of Egyptian rule, are somehow pursued by the assaults of temptations, which bring distress and fears and the most extreme dangers. Terrified by these, the minds of those newly grounded in the faith fall into complete despair of any good. But if Moses happens to be there, or one of the people's leaders who is like him, he will meet their fear with counsel and encourage their cowering minds with the hope of God's help. This could not happen unless the heart of the one in charge speaks to God. For many of those placed in such positions of leadership care only that outward appearances are well arranged; but of hidden things, which

…But it was not so with Moses. While he was telling the Israelites to take courage, he made no audible cry to God, and yet God himself testifies that he cried out. The word is teaching us, I think, that the voice which rings clearly and rises all the way to God's hearing is not a shout uttered with strain, but a thought sent up from a pure conscience. To someone in this state, his brother now seems a small help in the struggles he expects. I mean that brother who, by God's will, met Moses as he was going down to the Egyptians, and whom our account understood as having the rank of an angel. But it is then that the transcendent nature appears, showing itself as far as the one receiving it can contain it. The history tells us that this happened then, and the contemplation of the word teaches us that it happens always. When someone flees the Egyptian and, once outside the borders, grows afraid of the assaults of temptations, the guide shows him from above a salvation beyond all expectation. The enemy surrounds the one he is pursuing with all his forces, and so is forced to make the sea passable for him. Into the sea the guide leads the way: the cloud. That is the name of the guide, and those before us rightly took it to mean the grace of the Holy Spirit, through whom those who are worthy are guided toward the good. Whoever follows him passes through the water as the leader opens a path through it. Freedom is made secure in this way, because the one pursuing him into slavery is destroyed in the water. Who does not know that the Egyptian army stands for the various passions of the soul by which a person is enslaved? Those horses, those chariots and the riders on them, the archers, slingers, and heavy-armed soldiers, and the rest of the crowd in the enemy's battle line. How could anyone say that angry thoughts, or the impulses toward pleasure, grief, and greed, differ from that army? Abuse is plainly a stone from a sling, and the angry impulse is a spear brandishing its point. Let the horses be understood as the passion for pleasures, dragging the chariot along with unrestrained impulse. In the chariot ride the three men whom the history calls tristatai. You will surely understand these three borne by the chariot if you have already learned from the mystery of the doorposts and the lintel, and refer the meaning to the threefold division of the soul into the rational, the appetitive, and the spirited. All these, then, and everything akin to them, rush with the leader of the evil assault into the water after the Israelite. For them the nature of the water, led by faith in the staff and by the illuminating cloud, gives life to those who take refuge in it but destroys their pursuers. Through this the history teaches what kind of

…it is fitting that those who pass through the water should drag nothing of the opposing army along with them once they come up out of the water. For if the enemy comes up with a person, that person stays enslaved even after the water: he has brought the tyrant out alive with him, because he did not drown him in the deep. To put the riddle more plainly: all who pass through the mystical water in baptism must make the whole army of evil dead in the water. Greed, unbridled desire, the grasping mind, the passion of vanity and pride, the impulse of temper, anger, wrath, malice, envy: all these and things like them, since the passions somehow naturally follow our nature, must be made dead in the water, both the wicked movements of the mind themselves and what they produce. It is like the mystery of the Passover. Passover is the name of the sacrificial victim whose blood protects from death the one who uses it. There the law commands that the Passover be eaten with unleavened bread, and unleavened bread is bread not mixed with stale leaven. By this the law gives us to understand that no remnant of evil should be mixed into the life that follows. Instead, one who has broken the continuous chain of evils by a change for the better should begin the life that comes after from a fresh start. In the same way the law wants us here to drown every Egyptian, that is, every form of sin, in the saving baptism as in a deep, and to come up alone, dragging nothing foreign along with us in our life. This is what we hear through the history, which says that in the same water enemy and friend are told apart by death and life: the enemy is destroyed and the friend is given life. Yet many who have received the mystical baptism do not know the precepts of the law. They mix the old leaven of evil into the life that follows, and even after crossing the water they bring the Egyptian army along with them alive in their habits. Take someone who grew rich through robbery or injustice, or got some land by perjury, or lives with a woman through adultery, or dared some other forbidden thing in his life before the gift of baptism. If he goes on enjoying what came to him wrongly even after the washing, and thinks he has been freed from the slavery of sins, he is like a man who does not see that he is still bent under wicked masters. For unbridled passion is a savage and raging master, which torments the servile mind with pleasures as with whips. Greed is another such master. It gives its slave no rest. However much he works serving his master's orders, and however much of what he wants he acquires, he is always driven on to more. And everything else that is done through evil is a list of tyrants and masters. Whoever serves them, even if he happens to have passed through the water, has not yet, in my view at least, touched the mystical water, whose work is the destruction of the wicked tyrants.

But let us go on again to what comes next in the account. The one who has passed through the sea as we have understood it, and has seen in it the Egyptian dead as we have interpreted him, no longer looks to Moses alone, the staff-bearer of virtue. Instead, as before, he believes God, as the historical account says, and obeys God's servant Moses. We see this happening now among those who truly cross the water: having dedicated themselves to God, they also obey and submit to those who serve the Divine through the priesthood, as the Apostle says. After the sea comes a three days' journey. In it they camped at a certain place and found that the water there was at first undrinkable because it was bitter, but the wood put into it made the drink pleasant for the thirsty. The history matches what actually happens. A person who has left behind the Egyptian pleasures he served before crossing the sea at first finds a life separated from pleasures hard to accept and unpleasant. But if the wood is thrown into the water, that is, if someone receives the mystery of the resurrection, which had its beginning through the wood (and when you hear 'wood' you have surely understood the cross), then the life of virtue becomes sweeter and more refreshing than any sweetness that tickles the senses with pleasure, for it is sweetened by the hope of things to come. The next stopping place on the journey, rich with palm trees and springs, refreshes the travelers in their weariness. There are twelve springs of water, of a pure and very pleasant stream, and seventy palms, large and high-crowned, which time had raised to a great height. What do we find in these as the history continues in order? That the mystery of the wood, through which the water of virtue becomes drinkable for the thirsty, brings us to the twelve springs and the seventy palms, that is, to the teaching of the Gospel. In it the twelve springs are the apostles. The Lord chose that many for this service and made the word gush forth through them. One of the prophets foretold the grace that wells up from the apostles when he said, 'In the assemblies bless God the Lord, from the springs of Israel.' The seventy palms would be the apostles appointed throughout the whole world in addition to the twelve disciples, who were as many in number as the history says the palms were. But I think it fitting to hurry the journey along in our account. Through the few things we have set out, we have made the contemplation of the remaining encampments easy for the more diligent. The encampments would be virtues. In them the one who follows the pillar of cloud, advancing in order, pitches camp and rests. So I will pass over the stopping places in between and recall the miracle at the rock. Its hard and solid nature became drink for the thirsty when its hardness was dissolved into the softness of water.

It is no labor to fit the sequence of the history to the figurative contemplation. The one who has left the Egyptian dead in the water, who has been sweetened by the wood, who has delighted in the apostolic springs and rested in the shade of the palms, now becomes able to receive God as well. For the rock, as the Apostle says, is Christ. To unbelievers he is waterless and hard, but if someone applies the rod of faith, he becomes drink for the thirsty and flows into those who receive him. 'For I and my Father,' he says, 'will come and make our dwelling with him.' It is worth not passing this over without contemplation. After the sea was crossed, after the water was sweetened for the travelers of virtue, after that pleasant stay among the springs and palms, and after they drank from the rock, then the Egyptian provisions ran out completely. With no foreign food left of what they had brought as provisions from Egypt, food flowed down from above, food that was at once varied and uniform. In appearance [?] it was uniform, but its quality had variety, for it adapted itself to each person according to the kind of thing he desired. What then do we learn? We learn the purifications by which a person ought to cleanse himself of the Egyptian and foreign life. In this way he empties the sack of his soul of all the evil food the Egyptians prepare, and then receives into himself, with a pure soul, the food that comes down from above. No sowing produced this food for us by farming. It was bread ready-made, unsown and unplowed, coming down from above yet found on the earth. You surely perceive the true food through the riddle of the history: the bread that came down from heaven is not something incorporeal. How could the incorporeal become food for a body? And what is not incorporeal is certainly a body. Neither plowing nor sowing produced the body of this bread. The earth stayed just as it was and yet was found full of this divine food, which the hungry share in. Through this miracle they were being taught in advance the mystery of the Virgin. This unfarmed bread, then, is also the Word, which varies its power through the many forms of its quality to suit the needs of those who eat. It knows how to be not only bread but also milk, and meat, and vegetables, and whatever else suits and pleases those who take it. Paul the divine apostle teaches this, he who sets such a table for his own people. For the more mature he makes the word solid and meaty food, for the weaker vegetables, and for the infants milk. All the wonders the history tells about that food are teachings for the life of virtue. It says that everyone received an equal share of the food. The strength of the gatherers made no difference, and no one had more than he needed or less. In my view at least, this is a piece of advice set before everyone…

…not to go beyond the limits of need when they draw their means of living from these material things, but to know well that the natural measure of eating is the same for all: what is enjoyed for the day. Even if many times more than is needed is prepared, the stomach by nature cannot go beyond its own measure, nor does it stretch to match the greed of the provisions. As the history says, the one who took much did not have too much, for he has nowhere to put away the surplus, and the one who took little did not have too little, for his need shrank to what he found and was measured to it. For those who store up the excess, their greed turns into a breeding of worms. Through this the account in a way cries out to the greedy that everything beyond need, held on to by this greedy desire, becomes a worm on the following day, that is, in the life we await, for the one who stored it up. The hearer certainly understands by this worm the undying worm, which greed brings to life. That the stored portion lasted on the Sabbath alone without spoiling contains this advice: we should use the acquisitive disposition at the time when what is gathered does not admit corruption. It becomes useful to us when we have passed the preparation of this life and come into the rest from activity after death. For the day before the Sabbath both is and is called the Preparation for the Sabbath. This would be the present life, in which we make ready for ourselves the things of the life to come. In that life none of the works now allowed to us is done: not farming, not trade, not military service, nor anything else that people busy themselves with here. Instead, living free of all such works, we reap the fruits of the seeds we now sow in this life. They are incorruptible if the seeds of our life were good, but corrupting and deadly if the farming of this life produced such fruit for us. 'For whoever sows to the Spirit,' it says, 'will reap eternal life from the Spirit, but whoever sows to the flesh will reap corruption from the flesh.' Only the making ready for what is better is properly called Preparation and is sanctioned by the law, and what it stores up is incorruption. One would call the opposite not a preparation but a falling away from preparation. That is why the history lays down for people only the preparation that is achieved for the better, and by leaving the opposite unsaid it leaves it for the intelligent to understand. In military enlistments the commander first provides the rations and only then gives the signal for battle. In the same way, the soldiers of virtue first receive the mystical ration and then make war on the foreigners, with Joshua, the successor of Moses, leading the battle. Do you see the order in which the account proceeds? As long as a person is still weak and harmed by the wicked tyranny, he does not fight off the enemy by himself, because he cannot. Someone else champions the weak, the one who…

…strikes the enemy with blow after blow. But once he has been freed from slavery to those who ruled him, sweetened by the wood, rested from his weariness at the stopping place of the palms, has come to know the mystery of the rock and has shared in the heavenly food, then he no longer fights off the enemy through another's hand. Like someone who has passed beyond childhood and reached the prime of youth, he himself takes on his adversaries. And the general he has is no longer Moses, the servant of God, but God himself, whose servant Moses was. For the law, given at the beginning as a type and shadow of things to come, stays out of the fighting in the true contests. The one who leads as general is the fulfiller of the law and the successor of Moses, who was proclaimed in advance by sharing the name of the man who led the army then. When the people see the lawgiver's hands raised, they gain the upper hand over the enemy in battle; but when his hands are lowered, they give way. Moses' lifting his hands on high signifies the contemplation of the law through the loftiest thoughts. His letting them sink to the ground signifies the lowly, earthbound interpretation and observance of the law according to the letter. The priest holds up Moses' heavy hands, with the help of one who is related to him by birth. This too fits the sequence of what we have contemplated. For the true priesthood, through the divine word joined to it, lifts back up on high the workings of the law, which the heaviness of the Jewish mind had thrown to the ground. It props up with the stone the law that is falling to the ground, so that, standing upright with outstretched hands, the law shows its own purpose to those who look at it. For truly, to those who are able to see, the mystery of the cross is contemplated in the law above all. That is why the Gospel says somewhere that not an iota or a stroke of the law will pass away. By these it means the horizontal and the vertical line, with which the shape of the cross is drawn. This shape, seen at that time in Moses, who is understood to stand for the law, becomes the cause of triumph and victory for those who see it. Once again the account, by an orderly ascent, leads our mind by the hand to the higher reaches of virtue. The one who has been strengthened by the food, who has shown his strength in combat with his adversaries and has defeated those arrayed against him, is then brought to that ineffable knowledge of God. Through these things the account teaches us what kinds of things, and how many, must first be achieved in life before someone may dare to approach in mind the mountain of the knowledge of God. There he hears the sound of the trumpets, enters the darkness where God is, and has the divine characters engraved on the tablets. And if the tablets are broken through some fault, he presents to God again tablets cut by hand and has the divine finger engrave once more the letters recorded on the first ones. But it would be better to fit the meaning to the spiritual interpretation step by step, following the order of the history.

Consider the one who looks to Moses and to the cloud, both of which guide those who advance in virtue. In this part Moses would be the precepts of the law, and the cloud would be what goes before the law and leads the way [?]. This person has cleansed his mind in the crossing of the water and has killed and separated from himself what was foreign. He tastes Marah, that is, the life separated from pleasures, which at first seems bitter and unpleasant to those who taste it but becomes sweet to those who have received the wood. Then he delights in the beauty of the gospel palms and springs, is filled with the living water, which is the rock, and takes the heavenly bread into himself. He fights bravely against the foreigners, and the cause of his victory is the stretching out of the lawgiver's hands, which foreshows the mystery of the cross. When all this is done, he is brought to the contemplation of the transcendent nature. The way to such knowledge is purity. Not only must the body be purified by sprinklings, but the garments must also be washed clean of every stain with water. This means that whoever is to approach the contemplation of what truly is must be pure in every way, pure and unstained in both soul and body, having washed away the dirt of each in the way that suits it. Then we may appear pure to the one who sees what is hidden, and our outward decency may match the inner disposition of the soul. That is why, before the ascent of the mountain, the garments are washed at God's command: the riddle of the garments points us to the decent clothing of our life. No one would say that ordinary visible dirt on clothes hinders the ascent of those going up to God. Rather, I think the garment is rightly taken to mean the outward covering of the pursuits of this life. When this has been achieved, and the herd of irrational animals has been driven far from the mountain, he then approaches the ascent to lofty thoughts. In our view, the command that no irrational animal should appear on the mountain means that in the contemplation of intelligible things one rises above the knowledge that comes from the senses. For it is proper to the nature of irrational animals to be governed by sense alone, without understanding. Sight leads them, and hearing often stirs their impulse toward something. And everything else through which the senses act has great scope in irrational animals. But the contemplation of God does not come about through what is seen or what is heard, nor is it grasped by any of our usual concepts. For eye has not seen it, nor ear heard it, nor is it among the things that usually enter the human heart. Whoever is to approach the understanding of lofty things must first purify his way of life of every sensory and irrational impulse. He must wash from his mind every opinion that comes from some preconception, and separate himself from his usual intimacy with his own consort, that is, sense, which is in a way yoked to our nature and lives with it. Having become pure of this, he may then dare to climb the mountain. For truly steep and hard to approach is the mountain of…

…theology, whose foothills the great crowd of people barely reach. But if someone were a Moses, he would go up the ascent and take in with his ears the sounds of the trumpets, which the historical account says grew louder as they went on. Truly the proclamation about the divine nature is a trumpet that strikes the hearing. It seems great even at first, but at the end it is greater and reaches the hearing more deeply. The law and the prophets trumpeted the divine mystery of God's dealings in human form, but those first sounds were too weak to reach disobedient ears. That is why the dull hearing of the Jews did not take in the sound of the trumpets. But as the account says, the trumpets grew stronger as they went on. For the last sounds, those that came through the gospel preaching, reached the hearing, as the Spirit sounding through the instruments made the sound nobler and more forceful in what followed. The instruments sounding one spiritual note would be the prophets and apostles, of whom the psalm says that their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world. The multitude could not bear the voice that came from above. Instead they left it to Moses to learn the secrets himself and to teach the people whatever doctrine he learned through the teaching from above. This too is one of the arrangements in the Church. Not everyone should push forward to grasp the mysteries. Rather, they should choose from among themselves someone able to receive divine things and listen to him gladly, treating as trustworthy whatever they hear from the one initiated into divine things. 'For not all are apostles,' it says, 'nor all prophets.' But this is not observed now in many of the Churches. Many who still need purification from the way they have lived, unwashed and stained in the clothing of their life, relying on their irrational senses, dare the divine ascent. As a result they are thrown down by their own reasonings. For heretical notions are simply stones that bury the very inventor of the wicked doctrines. What does it mean that Moses entered the darkness and saw God in it? What is related now seems somehow contrary to the first theophany: then the Divine was seen in light, but now in darkness. Let us not think that this is out of tune with the sequence of our spiritual interpretation. Through these things the account teaches that the knowledge of piety is at first light for those in whom it arises. For what is understood as the opposite of piety is darkness, and turning away from darkness comes about through sharing in light. But as the mind advances, and through ever greater and more perfect attention comes to understand true comprehension, the closer it draws to contemplation, the more it sees that the divine nature cannot be seen. For it leaves behind all that appears, not only whatever [?]…

[?] what sense perceives, but also whatever the mind seems to see; it always presses on toward what lies deeper, until by the mind's tireless searching it slips through to what is unseen and incomprehensible, and there sees God. For the true knowledge of what is sought consists in this, and the seeing consists in this: in not seeing. What is sought lies beyond all knowledge, cut off on every side by incomprehensibility as if by a kind of darkness. That is why the sublime John, who entered this luminous darkness, says, "No one has ever seen God." By this negation he declares that knowledge of the divine essence is beyond the reach not only of human beings but of every intelligent nature. So when Moses had grown greater in knowledge, he declared that he saw God in darkness. This means that he then came to know that the Divine is by its nature that which is higher than all knowledge and comprehension. For Scripture says, "Moses entered into the darkness where God was." What God? The one who "made darkness his hiding place," as David says, who was initiated into ineffable things in that same sanctuary. Once he has arrived there, he is taught again through the darkness what he had been taught before through the darkness. In this way, I think, our teaching on this subject becomes firmer, since it is attested by the divine voice. For the divine word forbids from the very first that human beings should liken the Divine to anything known. Every concept that comes from some comprehensive image, by way of apprehending and conjecturing about the divine nature, fashions an idol of God and does not proclaim God. Now the virtue of piety is divided in two: what concerns the Divine, and the right ordering of one's conduct, since purity of conduct is also a part of piety. Moses first learned what one must know about God, and this knowing meant knowing nothing about him of what is known through human comprehension. Then he is taught the other kind of virtue, learning the practices by which the virtuous life is brought to perfection. After this he enters the tabernacle not made with hands. Who will follow a man who travels through such things and whose mind is lifted so high? Passing as it were from peak to peak, he climbs the heights and always becomes higher than himself. First he left the foot of the mountain, separating himself from all who were too weak for the ascent. Then, as he is lifted up with the height of the ascent, his ears receive the sound of the trumpets. After this he slips into the invisible inner sanctuary of the knowledge of God. Yet he does not stay even there, but passes on to the tabernacle not made with hands. Truly this is the goal reached by one who is lifted up through such ascents. For it seems to me that in another sense too the heavenly trumpet becomes, for the one who climbs, a teacher of the way into what is not made with hands. The ordered array of wonders in the heavens proclaims the wisdom displayed in all that exists and tells of God's great glory through what is visible, as the saying goes: "The heavens declare the glory of God." This array becomes a loud-voiced trumpet of clear and melodious teaching,

[St Gregory of Nyssa] as one of the prophets says, "God sounded the trumpet from above." Whoever has been purified and has sharp hearing in the heart receives this sound, I mean the sound that comes from contemplating what exists and leads to knowledge of the divine power. Guided by it, he penetrates with his mind to where God is. Scripture calls this "darkness," which signifies, as has been said, what is unknown and unseen. Having entered it, he sees that tabernacle not made with hands, which he shows to those below by means of a material copy. What, then, is that tabernacle not made with hands, which was shown to Moses on the mountain? He is commanded to look to it as an archetype, so that through a handmade structure he might display the wonder not made with hands. "See," it says, "that you make everything according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain." There were golden pillars set on silver bases and adorned in the same way with silver capitals. There were other pillars as well, whose capitals and bases were of bronze, while the part between the ends was silver. The core of all these was wood that does not rot. All around, to the eye, the brilliance of these materials was poured out. Likewise there was an ark gleaming with pure gold, and what supported its covering of gold was also wood that does not decay. Besides these there was a lampstand. It was a single shaft at its base but divided into seven branches at the top, and the branches held up an equal number of lamps. The lampstand was made of gold; no part of it was hollow, nor was it supported by wood. Besides these there was an altar and a mercy seat, and the so-called cherubim, whose wings overshadowed the ark. All of these were gold, and their gold was not a fine color laid over the surface. It was the same throughout, the material going all the way to the core. Besides these there were curtains richly worked by the weaver's art, with various colors interwoven one with another to make the fabric beautiful. They divided the part of the tabernacle that some of the priests could see and enter from the part that was inaccessible and not to be entered. The front part was called the Holy, and the hidden part the Holy of Holies. Besides these there were basins and censers, the enclosure of curtains outside, coverings of hair, and skins dyed red. What account could understand precisely all these things and everything else the narrative describes? Of what things not made with hands are these the copies? And what profit does the material copy of what Moses saw there bring to those who look at it? But it seems best to me to leave a precise account of these things to those who have the power, through the Spirit, to search the depths

of God, if indeed there is anyone like that, who can "speak mysteries in the Spirit," as the Apostle says. Whatever we say by way of conjecture about the meaning before us, we will leave to the readers' judgment. Each reader charged with judging may decide whether it should be rejected or accepted. We say, then, taking a brief starting point from what has been said, and since Paul has partly uncovered the mystery in these things, that Moses was instructed beforehand in a figure about the mystery of the tabernacle that encompasses the universe. This tabernacle would be Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God. In his own nature he is not made with hands, yet he allows himself to be constructed when this tabernacle must be pitched among us. So the same tabernacle is in a certain sense both unconstructed and constructed: uncreated in that it existed beforehand, and created in that it took on this material makeup. Perhaps what is said is not unclear to those who have accurately received the mystery of our faith. For there is one who [?] at the end of the ages came into being. He did not need to come into being in time, for how would he who exists before times and ages need a birth in time? But for our sake, since we had corrupted our being through folly, he accepted coming into being as we do, so that he might bring back into being what had fallen outside of being. This is the only-begotten God, who contains the universe in himself but also pitched his own tent among us. But if

so great a good is called a "tent," let the lover of Christ not be troubled at all, as though the connotation of the word made the greatness of God's nature smaller. For no other name is worthy of the nature of what it signifies either. All names alike fall short of precise meaning, both those thought to be lowly and those in which some grandeur of thought is seen. All the other names are each piously applied in some particular sense to indicate the divine power, such as physician, shepherd, protector, bread, angel, vine, way, door, dwelling, water, rock, spring, and whatever else is said of him. In the same way he is also called by the word "tabernacle," in a sense befitting God. For the power that encompasses all that exists, in which all the fullness of the Godhead dwells,

the common shelter of the universe, who contains everything in himself, is properly called a tabernacle. The vision must fit the name, and each thing seen must lead us by the hand toward the contemplation of some idea worthy of God. Now the great Apostle says that the veil of the lower tabernacle is the flesh, because, I think, flesh is made up of the four different elements. Perhaps he too had a vision of the tabernacle when, in the sanctuaries beyond the heavens,

the mysteries of paradise were revealed to him through the Spirit. If so, it would be well to attend to this partial interpretation and fit the whole contemplation of the tabernacle to it. The very words of the Apostle may make the riddles of the tabernacle clear to us. For he says somewhere about the Only-begotten, whom we have taken to be the tabernacle, that in him all things were created, visible and invisible, whether thrones or authorities or principalities or dominions or powers. Consider, then, the silver-gleaming and gold-wrought pillars, the carrying poles and rings, those cherubim that cover the ark with their wings, and everything else contained in the description of how the tabernacle was built. If one considers them with an eye to things above, they are the powers beyond the world, contemplated in the tabernacle, which support the universe by the divine will. These are our true carrying poles. They are sent out to serve for the sake of those who will inherit salvation. Passed as if through rings into the souls of those being saved, they raise up through themselves those who lie on the ground to the height of virtue. And when the text says that the cherubim cover with their wings the mysteries lying in the ark of the covenant, it confirms the interpretation of the tabernacle we have given. For we have learned that this name belongs to the powers contemplated around the divine nature, which Isaiah and Ezekiel beheld. Do not be surprised to hear that the ark of the covenant is covered by the wings. In Isaiah too one can learn the same thing, which the prophet says in a riddle about the wings. Here it is the ark that is covered, there the face, as though what is meant in both is one and the same. This, it seems to me, hints that the contemplation of things that cannot be spoken is beyond comprehension. And if you hear of lamps held up on many branches from a single lampstand, so that the light shining on every side is rich and abundant, you would not be wrong to think that the manifold radiance of the Spirit shines forth in this tabernacle. So Isaiah says, dividing the splendors of the Spirit into seven. The mercy seat, I think, needs no interpretation at all, since the Apostle has uncovered what was hidden when he says, "whom God put forward as a propitiation for our souls." And when you hear of the altar and the altar of incense, understand the worship that the heavenly beings continually offer in this tabernacle. For he says that not only the tongue of those on earth and under the earth, but also of those in heaven, sends up praise to the source of all things. This is the sacrifice pleasing to God, "the fruit of the lips," as the Apostle says, and the fragrance of prayers. And if skin dyed red and woven hair are also seen among these things, not even this will break the thread of our interpretation. For when the prophetic eye entered the vision of divine things, it beheld there the saving passion, determined beforehand,

which is signified by each of the things mentioned: the red signifies the blood, and the hair signifies death. For hair in the body has no share in sensation, which is why it properly becomes a symbol of death. When the prophet looks at the upper tabernacle, then, these are the things he sees through these figures. But one might contemplate the lower tabernacle. Since Paul often calls the Church "Christ," it would be well to say that these names refer to the ministers of the divine mystery, whom Scripture also calls pillars of the Church: apostles, teachers and prophets. For Peter, John and James are not the only pillars of the Church, nor was John the Baptist the only burning lamp. All who support the Church through themselves, and all who become lights through their own works, are called both pillars and lamps. "You are the light of the world," the Lord says to the apostles. And again the divine Apostle bids others to be pillars when he says, "Be steadfast and immovable." He also made Timothy into a fine pillar, making him, as he says in his own words, "a pillar and foundation" of the Church of truth. In this tabernacle the sacrifice of praise and the incense of prayer are seen offered continually, morning and evening. The great David gives us to understand this when he directs the incense of his prayer to God as a fragrant aroma and performs the sacrifice by lifting up his hands. Anyone who hears of basins will surely think of those who wash away the stain of sins through the mystical water. John was a basin, washing people in the Jordan with the baptism of repentance. Peter was a basin, leading three thousand people down to the water all at once. Philip was the basin for the servant of Candace. And all who administer this grace are basins for all who share in the gift. The curtains, which join together to enclose the tabernacle on every side, might be taken to mean the loving and peaceful harmony of believers, and whoever takes them so would not miss the fitting sense. For this is how David interprets it when he says, "who makes your borders peace." The red-dyed skin and the coverings of hair contribute to the beauty of the tabernacle. They could fittingly be understood as the putting to death of the sinful flesh, which the red-dyed skin figures, and the austere life of self-control. These especially adorn the tabernacle of the Church. Skins have no natural life-giving power in themselves, but the red dye makes them bright. This teaches that the grace which blossoms through the Spirit comes to no one unless they have made themselves dead to sin. Whether the text also means modest shame by the red dye, I leave to the judgment of anyone who wishes. The hair plaited together makes a rough, harsh fabric, and so it hints at

this rough self-control which wears away the passions that live with us. The life of virginity displays all such things in itself, since it keeps down the flesh of those who live in this way. The inner part, called the Holy of Holies, cannot be entered by the many. Let us not think that this is out of keeping with the sequence of what we have understood. For the truth of what exists is truly a holy thing, the holy of holies, something incomprehensible and inaccessible to the many. It is set in the innermost and secret recesses of the tabernacle of the mystery. So we must not pry into the understanding of things beyond comprehension. We must believe that what we seek exists, yet does not lie open before the eyes of all, but remains ineffable in the innermost recesses of the mind. Taught these and similar things through the vision of the tabernacle, that purified eye of Moses' soul was lifted up by such sights. It is raised again to the summit of other ideas, and is taught about the vestments of the priesthood. Among these are the undergarment and the overgarment, and that breastpiece shining with the varied splendor of its stones. There is the band around the head and the plate upon it, the breeches, the pomegranates and the bells. Then, above all, there are the oracle and the manifestation, the truth seen on both, and the shoulder pieces that fasten them on either side, engraved with the names of the patriarchs. The very names of the vesture spare us a lengthy and detailed interpretation of each item. For what bodily garment is called "manifestation," or "oracle," or "truth"? Clearly these names show that the narrative is not describing this visible clothing for us, but an adornment of the soul, woven by the practice of virtue. The full-length robe is dyed blue. Some who interpreted the text before us say that the dye signifies the air. For my part, I cannot firmly affirm whether such a shade of color is akin to the color of the air. Yet I do not reject the explanation, for the idea contributes to the contemplation of virtue. It means that the one who is to serve God as a priest must offer his own body in the sacred rite. He must become a victim that is not killed, in the living sacrifice and spiritual worship. He must not harm his soul with a thick and fleshy garment of life. Instead, through purity of life, he must make all the pursuits of life as fine as a spider's thread, and remake this bodily nature so that it comes close to what rises upward and is light and airy. Then, when we hear the last trumpet, we will be found weightless and light in answer to the voice of the one who calls. We will be carried aloft through the air together with the Lord, with no weight dragging us down to the earth. Whoever, then, following the Psalmist's counsel, has made his soul waste away like a spider has put on that airy tunic

that reaches from the head to the tips of the feet. For the law does not want virtue cut short. The golden bells, hung around the hem among the pomegranates, are the brilliance of good works. For there are two pursuits by which virtue is gathered: faith in God, and a conscience in how one lives. The great Paul adds these pomegranates and bells to Timothy's garment when he says that he must have faith and a good [?]

Let faith, then, ring out clear and loud in proclaiming the Holy Trinity. And let one's life imitate the nature of the pomegranate fruit. Its outside cannot be eaten, being enclosed in a hard and bitter rind. But what lies inside is pleasant to look at, with the fruit arranged in a varied and orderly way, and even more pleasant to taste, sweetening the sense. In the same way, the philosophical and austere way of life is hard to grasp and unpleasant to the senses, yet it is full of good hopes when it ripens into its own fruit. For when our gardener opens the pomegranate of life in its own season and shows the beauty of what was stored up within, then sharing in its fruits becomes sweet to those who enjoy them. For the divine Apostle says somewhere that all discipline seems for the present to bring not joy but pain. This is the part of the pomegranate that those who touch it meet first. "But afterward it yields a peaceful fruit." This is the sweetness of the edible parts within. The text also directs that this tunic be tasseled. Tassels are spherical pendants hung on for adornment, beyond what is needed. Through them we learn that virtue must not be measured by the commandment alone. We must also find something ourselves, devising additions from outside, so that some extra adornment is added to the garment. Paul was such a man, weaving his own fine tassels into the commandments. The law commands that those who serve at the altar share in the altar. It does not forbid taking along a sister as a wife, and it says that those who proclaim the Gospel should live by it. Yet he makes the Gospel free of charge, going hungry and thirsty and naked. These are the fine tassels that adorn the tunic of the commandments with additions of their own. Next, two cloths are laid over the full-length robe from above. They reach from the shoulders down over the chest and back, and are joined to each other by two clasps, one on each shoulder. The clasps are stones engraved with the names of the patriarchs, six on each. The weaving of the cloths is varied. Blue is interwoven with purple, and the red of scarlet is mingled with fine linen. Through all of these a gold thread is sown, so that from this many-colored dyeing a single blended beauty [?]

[?] to shine out. What we learn from these things is this: the upper parts of the vesture, all that properly serves as the adornment of the heart, are blended together from many different virtues. Blue is interwoven with purple, for kingship is joined to purity of life. Scarlet is interwoven with fine linen, because somehow the brightness and purity of a life naturally grow together with the blush of modesty. And the gold that shines among these colors hints at the treasure laid up for such a life. The patriarchs engraved on the shoulder-pieces contribute not a little to this adornment of ours, for human life is all the more beautified by the examples of good that have gone before. Again, over the adornment of the robes another adornment is laid from above: shields of gold hanging down on each of the shoulder-pieces and holding up between them a piece of goldwork in a square shape, glittering with twelve stones set in rows. There are four rows, each containing three stones. Among them you could not find one of the same kind as another; each was beautified by its own particular gleam. Such, then, is the form of the adornment. As for its meaning, the shields hanging from the shoulders hint at armor against the adversary that serves on both sides, as has been shown. As was said a little earlier, since virtue is achieved both through faith and through a good conscience in this life, one is secured on both sides by the protection of the shields and remains unwounded by such arrows, through the weapons of righteousness for the right hand and for the left. And that square ornament hanging from the shields on either side, on whose stones are inscribed the patriarchs who gave their names to the tribes, becomes a covering for the heart. The word teaches us that whoever has beaten off the evil archer with these two shields will adorn his own soul with all the virtues of the patriarchs, each shining out in its own way in the robe of virtue. And let the square shape be for you a sign of steadfastness in the good. For such a shape is hard to dislodge, since it rests on the straightness of its sides by means of equal angles. The straps by which these ornaments are bound to the arms seem to me to offer a teaching for the lofty life: that practical philosophy must be joined to the philosophy exercised in contemplation, so that the heart becomes a symbol of contemplation and the arms a symbol of works. The head adorned with the diadem signifies the crown laid up for those who have lived well, a crown adorned by the gold plate sealed with the ineffable characters. He puts no sandal on the one who has put on such adornment, so that he may not be weighed down for the race or hampered in his movement by a covering of dead skins, in keeping with the meaning found in the contemplation at the mountain. How then could the sandal become an ornament for the foot, when in the first initiation it was cast off as a hindrance to the ascent? And he who has passed through so much by the successive ascents we have contemplated carries in his hand the tablets made by God, which contain the divine law within them.

But these will be broken, shattered against the hard resistance of those who have sinned. The form of the sin was idol-making: the image was carved for the idolaters in the likeness of a calf. Moses ground it to powder, and it was wholly dissolved in the water and became drink for those who had sinned, so that the material that had served human impiety was in every way brought to nothing. In this the history then cried out prophetically above all about things that have now come to pass in our own time. For all the error concerning idols has been utterly obliterated, swallowed down by pious mouths, which through their good confession have brought about in themselves the destruction of the impious material. And the mysteries long established among the idolaters have become simply water, fleeting and insubstantial, water drunk down by the very mouths that once raved for idols. For when you see those who formerly fell into such vanity now destroying and obliterating the things in which they used to trust, does not the history seem to you to cry out plainly: Every idol will one day be swallowed by the mouths of those who have turned from deception to piety? Moses arms the Levites against their own people, and passing through the camp from one end to the other they carry out an indiscriminate slaughter of those they meet, entrusting the verdict on those slain to the edge of the sword. The killing fell equally on whoever happened to be there. It made no distinction among those being killed and paid no heed to enemy or friend, stranger or member of the household, kinsman or foreigner; there was one single impulse of the hand, acting alike against everyone it came upon. The account of this would give us the following benefit. Since the whole people agreed together in evil, and the entire camp became, as it were, a single one in the reckoning of wickedness, the scourge falls on them without distinction. For just as someone punishing with blows a person caught in wrongdoing lacerates with the whip whatever part of the body it happens to strike, knowing that the pain in one part passes through the whole, so too, as though the whole were being punished alike, since the body had grown together into wickedness, the scourge applied to a part chastened the whole. Therefore, if ever, when equal wickedness is seen in many, God's indignation acts not against all but against some, we should understand it as a correction worked out in love for humankind: not all are struck, but all are chastened by the partial blows into turning away from wickedness. But this is still the meaning of what is written according to the history. The spiritual sense would benefit us in this way. The lawgiver says in a proclamation common to all, 'If anyone is for the Lord, let him come to me.' This is the voice of the law commanding everyone: 'If anyone wishes to be a friend of God, let him become a friend to me, the law.' For whoever is a friend of the law is certainly also a friend of God. And he commands those gathered to him by such a proclamation to use the sword against brother and friend and neighbor. We understand, looking to the sequence

of the contemplation, that everyone who looks to God and to the law is purified by slaying what he has wrongly made his own. For Scripture does not understand every brother, friend or neighbor in the better sense. One may be both brother and stranger, friend and enemy, neighbor and one who stands against us. By these we understand the thoughts that have grown up together with us, whose life brings about our death and whose death brings about our life. This understanding agrees with what was examined earlier concerning Aaron. There, from his meeting with Moses, we understood the angel who is our ally and helper, the one who worked the signs against the Egyptians. He is fittingly understood as older, because the angelic and bodiless nature was created before ours, and as a brother, because of the kinship of that intelligible nature with our own intelligible nature. When the objection was raised how one could take in the better sense the meeting with Aaron, who became the Israelites' servant in making the idol, there too the word indicated in some measure that the name 'brother' is used in more than one sense: the same word does not always signify the same thing when the same name is applied to opposite meanings. One brother is he who overthrows the Egyptian tyrant; another, again, is he who fashions the idol for the Israelites, even though the name is the same for both. It is against such brothers, then, that Moses bares the sword. For what he commands others to do, he clearly prescribes for himself as well. The slaying of such a brother is the destruction of sin. For whoever destroys an evil that has been established in someone by the counsel of the adversary has killed in himself the one who once lived through sin. This teaching would be strengthened for us if we take some other details of the history along with this contemplation. For it is said that it was at the command of that Aaron that they had to take off their earrings, and their removal became the material for the idol. What do we say, then? That Moses adorned the hearing of the Israelites with the ornament of the ear, which is the law, but the falsely named brother, through disobedience, strips off the ornament placed on their hearing and makes an idol out of it. And at the first entry of sin, the counsel to disobey the commandment was a kind of removal of an earring. How did the first-formed humans come to regard the serpent as a friend and neighbor, when he counseled them to depart from the divine command as though it were something useful and good? That is what it means to take the earring of the commandment off the hearing. So whoever slays such brothers and friends and neighbors will hear from the law that voice which, the history says, Moses addressed to those who slew such people: 'You have filled your hands today for the Lord, each at the cost of his own son or brother, so that a blessing may be given to you.' And the remembrance of those who received sin seems to have entered the discussion at the right moment,

so that we may learn how, when the tablets made by God, on which the divine law had been engraved, fell to the ground from Moses' hands and were shattered by the hardness of what lay beneath, Moses brings them back again, no longer entirely the same, but only the writing on them. For he takes the tablets from the material here below and presents them to the power of the one who engraves the law on them. And so he recovers grace, carrying the law on stone tablets, God himself having imprinted the words on the stone. Perhaps, guided by these things, we may come to understand the divine providence on our behalf. For if the divine Apostle speaks truly when he calls the tablets hearts, that is, the ruling part of the soul (and he certainly does speak truly, since he searches the depths of God through the Spirit), we may learn from this by logical consequence that human nature was in the beginning unbroken and immortal, fashioned by the divine hands and beautified with the unwritten characters of the law, since the will that accords with the law was naturally present in us, in turning away from evil and in honoring the Divine. But when the sound of sin struck it, which the first Scripture calls the voice of the serpent and the history of the tablets calls the voice of those singing from wine, then it fell to the ground and was shattered. But again the true Lawgiver, of whom Moses was a type, hewed for himself from our earth the tablets of our nature. For it was not marriage that fashioned his divine flesh; he himself becomes the stonecutter of his own flesh, which was inscribed by the divine finger. For the Holy Spirit came upon the Virgin, and the power of the Most High overshadowed her. When this happened, our nature regained its unbroken state, becoming immortal through the characters written by the finger. For Scripture often calls the Holy Spirit the finger. And so Moses is transformed into greater glory, a transformation so great that the eye here below cannot bear the sight of that glory. Anyone who has been instructed in the divine mystery of our faith certainly knows how the spiritual contemplation agrees with the history. For the restorer of the broken tablet of our nature (you surely understand from what is said that I mean the one who healed our fractures) restored the broken tablet of our nature to its original state, beautified, as has been said, by the divine finger. Since then he can no longer be borne by the eyes of the unworthy, and the surpassing greatness of his glory makes him unapproachable to those who look upon him. For truly, when he comes, as the Gospel says, in his glory and all the angels with him, he will scarcely be bearable and visible even to the righteous. But the impious man, who holds the heresy of the Jews, remains, as Isaiah says, without share in that sight: 'Let the impious man be taken away,' he says, 'so that he may not see the glory of the Lord.' But in following the sequence of what we were examining, we were carried

into a conjecture about the contemplation of this passage. Let us return to the subject before us. How is it that one whom the divine voice testifies to have seen God clearly in so many theophanies (where it says, 'face to face, as a man speaks to his friend'), having reached such a state, asks God to appear to him, as though he had not yet attained what Scripture's testimony leads us to believe he had attained, and as though the one who was always appearing had not yet been seen? And the voice from above now agrees to the desire of the one who asks and does not refuse him the addition of this grace; yet again it leads him to despair by declaring that what he seeks cannot be borne by human life. Yet God says that there is a place beside him, and in the place a rock, and a hole in the rock, into which he commands Moses to go. Then God lays his hand over the mouth of the hole, and Moses, having come out, sees the back of the one who called him; and so he seemed to see the one he sought, and the promise of the divine voice proved true. If one looks at these things according to the letter, not only is their meaning unclear to those who inquire, but it will not even be free of an unfitting notion about God. For only things seen in a shape have a front and a back, and every shape is the boundary of a body. So whoever conceives of God as having a shape will not think him free even of bodily nature. Every body is certainly composite, and what is composite owes its existence to the coming together of things of different kinds. What has been put together no one could call indissoluble, and what is dissolved cannot be incorruptible, for corruption is the dissolution of what has been composed. If, then, someone understands God's back according to the letter, the logic will necessarily drive him into this absurdity. For front and back certainly belong to a shape, and shape to a body. And a body, by its own nature, can be dissolved. For everything composite is dissoluble, and what is dissolved cannot be incorruptible. So the slave of the letter would, by following his line of thought, conceive of corruption in God. Yet God is surely incorruptible and incorporeal. What meaning, then, other than the obvious one, will fit what is written? If this part of what is written in the context of the passage compels us to find another meaning, it is surely right to think the same about the whole. For as we understand the part, so we must necessarily take the whole as well. So the place beside God, the rock in the place, the opening in it called a hole, Moses' entry into it, the laying of the divine hand over its mouth, the passing by, the calling, and after these the sight of the back, will be more reasonably contemplated according to the rule of spiritual interpretation. What, then, is the meaning we infer? Just as heavy bodies, once they have received an impulse down a slope, even if no one pushes them after the first motion, are carried downward of themselves with ever greater speed, as long as the ground is inclined and

slopes downward beneath the moving body, and nothing is found to check the impulse by resisting it, so conversely the soul, once released from its attachment to earthly things, becomes light and swift in its upward motion, soaring from below toward the height. And since there is nothing above to cut off its impulse (for the nature of the good draws to itself those who look up to it), it always becomes higher than itself, straining forward, as the Apostle says, toward what lies ahead in its desire for heavenly things, and it will always direct its flight toward what is higher. For it longs not to lose, through what it has already attained, the height that lies beyond, and so it makes its upward course unceasing, always renewing its eagerness for flight through what it has already achieved. For only activity in accordance with virtue nourishes its strength by toil; it does not slacken its effort through the work but increases it. For this reason we say that the great Moses too, always growing greater, never halts in his ascent and sets himself no limit in his upward course. Having once set foot on the ladder on which God was set, as Jacob says, he always steps onto the rung above and never ceases to rise, because he always finds a rung beyond the height he has already reached. He refuses the false kinship with the queen of the Egyptians; he becomes the avenger of the Hebrew; he moves to the life of the desert, which human life had not disturbed; he shepherds within himself the flock of tame animals; he sees the radiance of the light; he makes his ascent to the light unburdened by taking off his sandal; he delivers his kinsmen and countrymen into freedom; he sees the enemy drowned, sinking beneath the waves. He camps under the cloud; he quenches thirst with the rock; he farms his bread from heaven. Then by stretching out his hands he overcomes the foreigner; he hears the trumpet; he enters the darkness; he slips into the inner sanctuary of the tabernacle not made with hands; he learns the secrets of the divine priesthood. He destroys the idol, appeases the Divine, recovers the law broken by the wickedness of the Jews, and shines with glory. And though lifted up to such heights, he still burns with desire and is insatiable for more. He still thirsts for that with which he was always filled as much as he wished, and as though he had not yet partaken of it, he asks to attain it, begging God to appear to him, not in the measure in which he is able to partake, but as God is. It seems to me that he feels this because his soul is moved by a kind of passionate love for what is beautiful by nature. Hope continually draws such a soul from the beauty it has seen to what lies beyond, always kindling its desire for what is hidden through what it continually grasps. Hence the ardent lover of beauty, receiving what always appears as an image of what he longs for, yearns to be filled with the very stamp of the archetype. And this is the meaning of the bold request, which goes beyond the limits of desire: to enjoy the beauty not through mirrors and reflections, but face to face

[?] But the divine voice grants what was asked through the very words by which it refuses, and in a few words it reveals an immeasurable depth of meaning. God's generosity agreed to fulfil his desire, but it did not promise that the longing would ever stop or be satisfied. For he would not have shown himself to his servant if the sight were such as to put an end to the beholder's desire, since truly seeing God consists in this: that the one who looks up to him never ceases to desire. For he says: "You cannot see my face; for no one shall see my face and live." The text does not mean that the face becomes a cause of death to those who see it. How could the face of Life ever be a cause of death to those who come near? Rather, the Divine is life-giving by nature, and the distinctive mark of the divine nature is to lie beyond every distinguishing mark. So whoever thinks that God is one of the things that can be known has turned away from what truly is towards what he imagines exists through a mental grasp, and he does not have life. For what truly is, is true life, and this cannot be reached by knowledge. If, then, the life-giving nature lies beyond knowledge, whatever is grasped is certainly not life, and what is not life does not have it in its nature to give life. So Moses' longing is fulfilled through the very fact that his desire remains unfulfilled. For he is taught by these words that the Divine is by its own nature infinite, enclosed by no boundary. If the Divine were thought of as having some boundary, it would be absolutely necessary to consider what lies beyond it together with the boundary, for whatever is bounded must end in something, as air is the boundary of land animals and water that of creatures living in water. A fish is enclosed by water on all its edges, and a bird by air. Between the water and the swimmer, or between the air and the bird, lies the outermost surface of the boundary that encloses the bird or the fish, and beyond it comes the water or the air. In the same way, if the Divine were thought of as having a boundary, it would necessarily be enclosed by something different from it in nature. And the logic of the argument shows that what encloses is many times greater than what it contains. Now it is agreed that the Divine is by nature good, and what differs in nature from the good is certainly something other than the good, and what lies outside the good belongs to the nature of evil. And it was shown that what encloses is many times greater than what is enclosed. So those who think that the Divine has a boundary must also admit that it is enclosed by evil. And since everything enclosed is smaller than what encloses it, it would follow that the greater prevails. Whoever confines the Divine within a boundary therefore makes the good subject to its opposite. But this is absurd. So no comprehension of the invisible nature can be conceived, and what cannot be encompassed cannot by its nature be grasped. Yet every desire for the good that is drawn towards that ascent always grows stronger along with the course that presses on towards the good. And this is truly to see God: never to find that one's desire is satisfied. One must always look through what one is able to see and be set on fire with the desire to see more. And so no limit could cut short

the growth of the ascent to God, because no limit of the good is ever found, and no satisfaction ever cuts short the progress of the desire for the good. But what is that place which is understood to be beside God? What is the rock? And again, what is the cleft in the rock? What is the hand of God that covers the mouth of the hollow in the rock?
