What is God's passing by? And what is his back, which God promised to give to Moses when he asked to see him face to face? Each of these must certainly be something great and worthy of the generosity of the giver. This promise should be believed to be more magnificent and more exalted than every manifestation of God that had already been granted to his great servant. How, then, could one understand from these words the height that Moses longs to climb after so many ascents, the ascent that he who works all things together for good for those who love God makes easy by his guidance? "Behold," he says, "a place beside me." This meaning perhaps agrees with what we have already considered. For in saying "place" he does not confine what is shown within a quantity, since what has no quantity has no measure. Instead, by using the image of a measured outline, he leads the hearer to what is infinite and unbounded. The text, then, seems to suggest something like this: "Since your desire is set on what lies ahead, and you never have your fill of the race, nor know any point at which you have had enough of the good, but your longing always looks towards more, the place beside me is so great that whoever runs in it can never come to the end of the race." But in another sense this race is a standing still. "For I will set you," he says, "upon the rock." And this is the most paradoxical thing of all: that the same thing is both standing still and moving. Someone who is climbing is certainly not standing still, and someone who stands still does not climb. Yet here the climbing happens through the standing. This means that the more firmly and immovably one remains in the good, the further one advances on the course of virtue. Someone who is unsteady and liable to slip, who stands insecurely in the good because his reasoning gives him no firm footing, who is tossed by the waves and carried about, as the Apostle says, and who doubts and wavers in his opinions about reality, would never run up to the height of virtue. He is like people walking uphill through sand: even if they take great strides, they labour in vain, because their footing keeps sliding down with the sand, so that there is movement but the movement brings no progress. But suppose someone, as the psalm says, draws his feet up out of the mire of the deep and plants them firmly on the rock, and the rock is Christ, perfect virtue. Then the more steadfast and immovable he becomes in the good, as Paul counsels, the faster he completes the race. He uses his standing as a kind of wing, and his heart takes wing for the journey upward through his steadiness in the good. So he who showed Moses the place urges him on to run the race, and by promising that he would stand on the rock he shows him the way to run that divine course. And the cleft in the rock,

which the text calls a "hole", the divine Apostle interpreted well in his own words, when he said that a heavenly house not made with hands is laid up in hope for those who have taken down their earthly tent. For truly, whoever has finished the race, as the Apostle says, in that broad and spacious stadium which the divine voice calls "place", and has kept the faith, or, as the riddle puts it, has planted his feet on the rock, will be adorned with the crown of righteousness by the hand of the judge of the contest. Scripture names this prize in various ways. Here the same thing is called a cleft in the rock. Elsewhere it is called the delight of paradise, the eternal tent, the dwelling with the Father, the bosom of the patriarch, the land of the living, the water of rest, the Jerusalem above, the kingdom of heaven, the prize of the calling, the crown of graces, the crown of beauty, the tower of strength, the joy of the banquet table, sitting in council with God, the throne of judgement, the renowned place and the hidden tent. We say, then, that Moses' entry into the rock is also one of the things that point to this meaning. Paul understood the rock to be Christ, and all hope of good things is believed to lie in Christ, in whom, as we have learned, are all the treasures of good things. So whoever comes to be in any good thing is certainly in Christ, who contains every good. Whoever has reached this point is sheltered by the hand of God, as the text promised. The hand of God would be the power that created all things, the only-begotten God, through whom all things came to be. He is also a place for those who run, for he becomes the way of the race, as he himself says; he becomes a rock for those who stand firm and a house for those who rest. Then such a person will hear the one who calls him and will come to be behind the one calling, that is, he "will walk after the Lord God," as the law commands. The great David also heard and understood this when he said to the one who dwells in the help of the Most High, "He will overshadow you with his back." This is the same as being behind God, for the back is behind. And he cries out about himself, "My soul has clung behind you; your right hand has upheld me." You see how the psalm agrees with the history. David says that the right hand gives help to the one who clings behind God. In the same way, in the history, the hand touches the one who waits in the rock for the divine voice and prays to follow behind. Indeed, the Lord himself, who spoke to Moses then and became the fulfiller of his own law, says the same thing to his disciples, laying bare and making plain the meaning of what had been said in riddles: "If anyone wishes to come after me." He does not say, "If anyone wishes to go before me." And to the man who pleads with him about eternal life he proposes the same thing: "Come," he says, "follow me." And whoever follows sees the back. So Moses, who is eager to see God, is now taught how one can

see God: to follow God wherever he leads is to see God. For his passing by signifies that he guides the one who follows. Someone who does not know the way cannot travel it safely except by following behind his guide. The guide, by going ahead, shows the follower the way, and the follower will not stray from the straight path as long as he keeps looking at the leader's back. Whoever turns aside, or turns his eyes to face his guide, cuts out a new path for himself, not the one the guide is showing. That is why he says to the one he is guiding, "My face shall not be seen by you," that is, do not stand face to face with your guide. For then your course would certainly run in the opposite direction. Good does not look the good in the face; it follows. What faces the good is understood to be its opposite. For vice looks at virtue from the opposite side, but virtue is not seen facing virtue. So Moses does not look God in the face; he sees his back. For whoever faces him will not live, as the divine voice testifies: "No one shall see the face of the Lord and live." You see how great a thing it is to learn to follow God. After those lofty ascents and those awesome and glorious appearances of God, near the very end of his life, the one who has learned to be behind God is barely found worthy of this grace. And once someone follows God in this way, none of the obstacles that come through vice stands in his way any longer. For after this, envy springs up against him from his brother and sister. Envy is the passion that began all evil, the father of death, the first entrance of sin, the root of vice, the birth of grief, the mother of misfortunes, the ground of disobedience, the beginning of shame. Envy drove us out of paradise when it became a serpent against Eve. Envy walled us off from the tree of life, stripped us of our holy garments and brought us in shame to the branches of the fig tree. Envy armed Cain against his own kin and invented the death that is avenged sevenfold. Envy made Joseph a slave. Envy is the deadly sting, the hidden weapon, the disease of nature, the bitter poison, the wasting we bring on ourselves, the cruel arrow, the nail in the soul, the fire in the heart, the flame burning in the bowels. For envy, misfortune is not its own evil but someone else's good, and success, by contrast, is not its own good but a neighbour's evil. Envy is pained by other people's good fortune and tramples on their misfortunes. They say that vultures, which feed on corpses, are killed by perfume, for their nature is at home with what is foul-smelling and rotten. So too whoever is gripped by this disease is destroyed by his friends' prosperity as if by a whiff of perfume. But if he sees someone suffering from a misfortune, he swoops down on it and brings his hooked beak to bear, dragging out the hidden parts of the calamity. Envy defeated many before Moses. But when it was hurled against this great man, it shattered itself, like a clay pot dashed against a rock. For this above all showed what Moses gained from his journey with God,

he who ran in the divine place, stood on the rock, was enclosed in its cleft, was sheltered by the hand of God, and followed behind his leader, not facing him but seeing his back. Following God, then, proves that the one who has reached this state is blessed, and shows that he stands too high for the bow's arrow to reach him. For envy shoots its arrow at him too, but the shot does not reach the height where Moses was. The bowstring of wickedness was too weak to shoot the passion far enough for it to pass to him from those who had already caught the sickness. Aaron and Miriam were wounded by the passion of jealousy and became a kind of bow for envy, shooting words against him instead of arrows. But Moses was so far from sharing the sickness that he even healed the passion of those who had caught it. Not only did he remain unmoved, seeking no revenge on those who had wronged him, but he even begged God to be merciful to them. By what he did he showed, I think, that whoever is well protected by the shield of virtue is not even scratched by the points of the arrows. For the hardness of the armour blunts the point and turns it back. And the armour that protects against such arrows would be God himself, whom the soldier of virtue puts on. "Put on," he says, "the Lord Jesus." This is the unbreakable armour. Protected by it, Moses made the wicked archer powerless. His anger against those who had wronged him was so blunted that, even when they had been condemned by the impartial judgement, he did not forget what he owed to his own kin, but became a suppliant to God on behalf of his brother and sister. He would not have done this if he had not been behind God, who had shown him his back to guide him safely along the path of virtue. And the events that follow are of the same kind. Since the enemy of human nature found no way to harm him, he turned his attack against those who were easier to capture. He let loose the passion of gluttony on the people like an arrow and made them become Egyptians in their appetite, so that they preferred the meat that the Egyptians ate to that heavenly food. But Moses, lofty in soul, soared above such a passion and was wholly intent on the inheritance to come. God had promised it to those who leave Egypt, understood spiritually, and journey towards that land in which milk flows mingled with honey. For this reason he made certain spies teachers about the good things there. In my view, those who held out good hopes would be the thoughts that arise through faith, confirming the hope of the good things laid up for us. Those who brought despair of the better hopes would be the thoughts that come from the Adversary, which blunt faith in what has been promised. But Moses paid no attention to the contrary reports and considered trustworthy the one who promised better things about that land. Joshua was the leader of the better report, and by his own assurance he made what had been promised believable. Looking to him, Moses held firm hopes about the future, taking as a sample of the delights there the cluster of grapes

that Joshua carried on poles. And when you hear of Joshua, that is, Jesus, reporting about that land, and of a cluster hanging from wood, you understand what Moses himself was looking to that made him secure in his hopes. For who else is the cluster hanging on wood but the cluster that was hung on the wood in the last days, whose blood becomes a saving drink for those who believe? Moses foretold this to us in a riddle: "They drank wine, the blood of the grape," by which the saving passion is signified. Again the way leads through the desert, and the people, who have despaired of the good things promised, are worn down by thirst. But Moses again floods the desert for them through the rock. Such a story, understood spiritually, would teach us what the mystery of repentance is. Those who once tasted the rock and then turned aside to the belly, the flesh and the pleasures of Egypt are condemned to a famine [?] of any share in good things. But through repentance they can find again the rock they abandoned, open up its vein for themselves once more and be filled again with the stream. The rock pours it out for whoever believes that Joshua's report is truer than that of his opponents, and looks up to the cluster that dripped blood for us and was bloodied, and who made the rock gush for them again through the wood. But the people had not yet been trained to follow in the footsteps of Moses' greatness. They are still dragged down towards slavish desires and lean towards the pleasures of Egypt. Through these events the history somehow shows that human nature is drawn down towards this passion more than any other, and is led into the disease by countless paths. For this reason Moses, like a physician who uses his skill always to combat whatever illness prevails, does not allow the disease to overpower them to the point of death. In some, the desire for unseemly things gave birth to serpents, and their bite brought deadly venom to those who were wounded. But the great lawgiver, by means of the image of a serpent, made the power of the real beasts useless. It is time to reveal the riddle more clearly. There is one remedy against these evil passions: the cleansing of our souls that comes through the mystery of godliness. And the heart of what is believed in this mystery is looking to the passion of him who accepted the passion for our sake. The passion is the cross, so that whoever looks to it, as the text teaches, is not harmed by the venom of desire. To look to the cross means to make one's whole life dead and crucified to the world, unmoved by any sin, nailing one's own flesh with the fear of God, as the Prophet says. The nail that holds the flesh fast would be self-control. The desire for unseemly things draws deadly serpents out of the earth, for every offspring of wicked desire is a serpent. For this reason the law shows us beforehand what appears on the wood. This is the likeness of a serpent and not [Deut. [?]; [?] 3:8]

[?]…serpent; as the divine Paul says, "in the likeness of sinful flesh." The true serpent is sin, and whoever deserts to sin takes on the serpent's nature. So humanity is set free from sin through the one who took on the form of sin and became like us, who had turned into the form of the serpent. Through him death from the bites is prevented, but the beasts themselves are not destroyed. By beasts I mean the desires. For in those who look to the cross, the evil death of sinners does not take effect, but the desire of the flesh that is set against the spirit has not wholly perished. Indeed, even in the faithful the bites of desire are often active; but whoever looks to the one lifted up on the wood drives off the passion, dispersing the venom with the fear of the commandment as with a medicine. The voice of God clearly teaches that the serpent lifted up in the wilderness is a symbol of the mystery of the cross, when it says: "As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up." Once again sin goes on its own way in a kind of evil sequence, moving forward step by step as though along a wicked chain; and the lawgiver, like a physician, extends the treatment alongside the course of the disease. For since the serpents' bite had become harmless to those who looked to the likeness of the serpent (you surely grasp the riddle from what has been said), another method of sin is devised by the one who contrives such things against us in many ways. This can be seen happening even now in many people. When some have chastened the passion of desire by a more temperate life, they thrust themselves into the priesthood, outraging God's ordinance by human canvassing and self-appointed ambition. The one whom the history accuses of working evil on human beings leads them into this evil sequence of sin. For when, through faith in the one lifted up on the wood, the earth ceased to bring forth serpents against those who desire, and they were persuaded that they were stronger than the venomous bites, then, as the passion of desire withdrew, the disease of arrogance came in to take its place. Judging it a lowly thing to keep to the rank in which they had been placed, they thrust themselves into the dignity of the priesthood,

[?]…the truth of what is recorded confirms our definition. For if those who raised themselves above others sank down somewhere below when the earth split open in a chasm, no one could fault the definition that calls arrogance the lowest fall. Looking at these things, Moses teaches us to be modest and not to be puffed up by our achievements, but always to keep our present state well ordered. It does not follow that, because you have become stronger than pleasures, you may now be caught by another kind of passion without being held to account. Every passion is a fall, so long as it is a passion, and there is no difference between falls in the variety of passions. Whoever slips on the smoothness of pleasure has fallen; and whoever is tripped up by arrogance has been overthrown. No kind of fall is to be chosen by anyone with sense; every fall is equally to be shunned, so long as it is a fall. So if you see someone even today who is to some extent clean of the sickness of pleasure, yet who, out of eagerness to seem above others, thrusts himself into the priesthood, consider that you are looking at that very man who falls from the height of arrogance. For in what follows the law teaches that the priesthood is something divine and not human. It teaches this way: Moses marks rods from each tribe with the names of those who gave them and sets them before the altar, so that the rod made distinguished from the others by a divine miracle might become a testimony to the appointment from above. When this was done, the rods of the others stayed what they were; but the priest's rod, taking root in itself, not through any moisture from outside but through the power placed in it by God, put forth branches and fruit, and the fruit came to ripeness. The fruit was a nut. When this happened, all the people under him were taught good order. We should understand from the fruit that the priest's rod produced what the life of the priesthood ought to be: self-controlled, austere and hard-shelled in its outward appearance, but holding within, hidden and unseen, what is edible. This is revealed when the food has ripened with time, the bitter rind has split open, and the woody covering of the edible part has been worn away. But if you learn that the life of someone called a priest is like an apple, fragrant and rosy, like many who deck themselves out in fine linen and purple, grow fat at rich tables, drink strained wine, anoint themselves with the finest perfumes, and enjoy whatever else seems sweet to the immediate taste of those who define life as enjoyment, you might well apply the Gospel saying to him: "Seeing the fruit, I do not recognize from the fruit the priestly tree." The fruit of the priesthood is one thing, and this is another. That fruit was self-control; this is luxury. That fruit was not fattened by earthly moisture; but into this many channels of pleasure flow from below, by which the produce of such a life reddens to its ripeness. When the people had become clean of this passion too, they passed through the land of foreigners, with the law leading them along the royal highway and keeping them from turning aside to either side.

For turning aside to either side is dangerous for the traveler. If two precipices narrow a single path along the top of a ridge, whoever walks it is in danger of turning aside from the middle one way or the other, for on both sides alike the abyss below the cliff awaits the one who strays. In the same way the law wants the one who follows in its footsteps not to leave the road which, as the Lord says, is narrow and hard, turning neither to the left and sinister side nor to what is reckoned the right. This teaching is a doctrine which holds that the virtues are found in a mean, since every vice naturally works either by falling short of virtue or by overshooting it. In the case of courage, for example, cowardice is a falling short of virtue and rashness an excess; what is free of both is found in the middle between the vices that lie beside it, and that is virtue. In the same way all the other things we strive for in pursuit of the better are somehow hemmed in by evil neighbors. Wisdom holds the mean between cunning and simplicity. Neither the serpent's shrewdness nor the dove's simplicity is praiseworthy if either one were to be chosen [?] on its own; but the disposition blended from the middle of these two becomes virtue. One who falls short in temperance is licentious; one who goes too far has his conscience seared, as the Apostle puts it. The first pours himself shamelessly into pleasures; the second loathes marriage as much as adultery. The disposition found between these is temperance. As the Lord says, this world lies in the evil one, and what opposes virtue, namely wickedness, is foreign to those who follow the law. So whoever journeys through this world in this life will safely complete this necessary journey of virtue if he keeps to the true highway, the road that virtue has worn smooth and made white, never turning aside through vice to the trackless ground beside it. But, as has been said, the scheming of the adversary climbs alongside the ascent of virtue, finding suitable occasions for each person to turn aside to evil. So when the people had grown greater in the life that accords with God, the adversary takes up another plot. He acts like those skilled in war who, seeing that a frontal battle against forces stronger than their own is hard to win, outmaneuver the enemy with tricks and ambushes. In the same way the army of evil, facing those strengthened by law and virtue, no longer leads its forces out face to face, but carries out its plot in secret through ambushes. So it calls in sorcery as an ally against those it is plotting against. The history says there was a soothsayer and augur who, through some working of demons, had a power that could harm his opponents. He was hired by the ruler of the Midianites to harm by cursing those who live for God, but he turned the curse into a blessing. Following on from what we have already considered, we understand that not even sorcery has any power against those who live in virtue; those who feast on divine help prevail over every plot.

The history attests that the man in question practiced divination by augury when it says that he had the fees of divination in hand and consulted the birds; and, before that, that he was given instruction about the undertaking before him through the braying of his ass. Scripture told of its cry as though it were articulate speech, because he habitually consulted the voices of irrational animals through some demonic working. In this way it shows that those who have been taken in by such deception of demons go so far as to accept as speech the instruction they get from the voices of animals through some kind of observation. As he paid attention, he learned through the very things by which he was being defeated the invincible power of those against whom he had been hired. In the Gospel story too, the band of demons, the legion, had been drawn up to resist the Lord's authority. But when the one who has power over all drew near, it cried out his surpassing power and did not hide the truth, that this is the divine nature, who at the appointed times will bring punishment on sinners. For the voice of the demons says: "We know who you are, the Holy One of God," and "You have come before the time to torment us." The same thing happened then, when the demonic power that attended the soothsayer taught Balaam that the people were invincible and could not be resisted. Fitting the history to what we examined earlier, we say that whoever wishes to curse those who live in virtue can utter no hurtful or unseemly sound, but turns the curse into a blessing. The meaning is this: the blame of reproach does not touch those who live according to virtue. How can someone who owns nothing be reproached for greed? How will anyone spread rumors of profligacy about someone who lives withdrawn and apart, or of anger about the meek, or of conceit about the humble, or of anything else blameworthy about those known for its opposite? Their aim is to offer a life that blame cannot lay hold of, so that, as the Apostle says, the opponent may be put to shame, having nothing to say. That is why the voice of the man hired to curse says, "How shall I curse one whom the Lord does not curse?" That is: How shall I reproach one who has given no material for reproach, whose life cannot be wounded by evil because it looks to God? Yet though the inventor of evil failed in this, he did not give up scheming against those he plots against altogether. He turns his scheming to his own special kind of wrestling, again luring nature to evil through pleasure. Pleasure truly is held out as a kind of bait for every evil, and it easily draws the greedier souls onto the hook of destruction. Above all, it is through licentious pleasure that nature is swept off unguarded into evil. And this is what happened then. Those who had prevailed over arms, who had shown every assault of iron to be weaker than their own strength, and who had routed the enemy's phalanx by force, were wounded by

the darts of women through pleasure. They proved stronger than men but weaker than women. The moment the women appeared to them, holding out their beauty in place of weapons, they at once forgot the vigor of their courage and let their spirit melt into pleasure. They were in the state one would expect of those maddened for unlawful union with foreigners. But familiarity with evil meant estrangement from the alliance of the good, for the Divine at once became their enemy. The zealous Phinehas, however, did not wait for the sin to be purged by a verdict from above; he himself became judge and executioner at once. Moved to anger against the frenzied, he fulfilled the priest's work by cleansing the sin with blood. It was not the blood of some innocent animal that had no share in the defilement of licentiousness, but of those joined to each other in wickedness. His spear passed through the two bodies and calmed the stirring of divine justice, mixing the pleasure of the sinners with their death. The history seems to me to lay down advice that profits the soul. It teaches us that, though there are many passions that overpower human thoughts, no other passion has strength against us to equal the disease of pleasure. Those Israelites had shown themselves stronger than the Egyptian cavalry, had overcome the Amalekites, had appeared fearsome to the nation after them, and afterward had prevailed over the phalanx of the Midianites. That these men were enslaved to the disease at the mere sight of foreign women shows nothing else, as has been said, than that pleasure is an enemy hard to fight and hard to resist. By merely appearing, it conquered those whom arms had not defeated and raised over them a trophy of dishonor, exposing their shame publicly with the daylight as witness. By itself it turned men into beasts, persuading them through the brutish and irrational impulse toward licentiousness to forget their human nature. They did not hide the abomination but paraded in the dishonor of the passion and prided themselves on the defilement of their shame, wallowing like swine in the mire of uncleanness openly before each other's eyes. What, then, does the story teach us? That, having learned how much power the disease of pleasure has to lead to evil, we should move our own life as far as possible from such a neighborhood, so that the disease may find no way in against us, like fire that kindles its wicked flame by being near. Solomon teaches this in the Wisdom when he says not to touch a hot coal with a bare foot or to put fire in one's bosom. It is in our power to remain free of passion as long as we are far from what sets us alight; but if we come so close as to touch its burning heat, the fire of desire will be in our bosom, and then burning will follow for the foot and ruin for the bosom. In the Gospel the Lord, in his own voice, so that we might be kept far from such an evil, cut out the desire that comes through seeing as if it were a root of the passion. He teaches that whoever admits the passion through the eyes opens a way for the disease against himself. For the evil of the passions, like a plague, once it has seized the vital parts, ends only with death. But I think there is no need to lengthen the discourse, since we have set the whole life of Moses before our readers as a pattern of virtue. For

to one who has stretched himself toward a loftier life, what has been said will be no small provision for the true philosophy. But for one who grows faint before the sweat of virtue, even if many times as much were written, no benefit would come of the labor. However, we must not forget what we laid down in the prologue, where our discourse maintained that the perfect life is one whose progress is hindered by no limit of perfection, and that the continual growth of life toward the better is the soul's way to perfection. So it would be well to carry the discourse to the end of Moses' life and show that the definition of perfection given us is secure. For the one who was raised up through so many ascents throughout his whole life never lacked a way to become higher than himself again. Thus, I think, his life may be seen in everything to soar like an eagle, above the clouds and aloft, circling in the upper air of spiritual ascent. He was born at a time when being born a Hebrew was considered a crime among the Egyptians. While the tyrant was then punishing newborns by law, he overcame that murderous law and was saved, first by his parents and afterward by the very people who had made the law. Those whose law had sought his death took every care not only for his life but for a life of distinction, training the young man in all wisdom. After this he rose above human honor and higher than royal rank, judging it stronger and more kingly to have virtue as his guard instead of bodyguards, and to take pride in its adornment instead of royal finery. Next he rescues his kinsman and strikes down the Egyptian with a blow; by careful contemplation we understand these as the soul's friend and its enemy. Then he makes stillness his teacher of lofty lessons, and so his mind is enlightened by the light that shone from the bush; and then he is eager to share with his kinsmen the good things God has given him. In these deeds he displayed his power in two ways: in defense against his opponents, by many successive plagues; and in kindness toward his kinsmen. He leads so great a people through the sea on foot, not by fitting out a fleet of ships for himself but by building them faith for the crossing. He makes the deep dry land for the Hebrews and keeps the sea a sea for the Egyptians. He sang the song of victory; he was guided by the pillar; he was enlightened by the heavenly fire; he set a table for himself with food from above. He was filled from the rock; he stretched out his hands for the destruction of the Amalekites. He climbs the mountain, enters the darkness, hears the trumpet, draws near to the divine nature, is enclosed by the heavenly tabernacle, adorns the priesthood, pitches the tabernacle, sets life right by laws, and wins the last wars in the way described. At the end of his achievements he punished licentiousness through the priesthood. For this is what the [?] carried out through Phinehas against the passion

For turning aside toward either side is dangerous for the traveller. Suppose two cliffs squeezed a single path along the top of a ridge. Whoever walks it is in danger of straying from the middle on one side or the other, for on either side the chasm below the cliff waits for anyone who strays. In the same way the law wants the one who follows in its footsteps not to leave the road which, as the Lord says, is narrow and hard, turning neither to the left and sinister side nor to what is thought to be the right. This teaching is a doctrine that defines the virtues as found in a mean, because every vice naturally works either by falling short of virtue or by going beyond it. In courage, for example, cowardice is a falling short of virtue and rashness an excess. What is free of both is found in the middle between the vices on either side, and that is virtue. In the same way, everything else that is pursued for the sake of the better is somehow hemmed in between bad neighbours. Wisdom holds the mean between cunning and simplicity. Neither the shrewdness of the serpent nor the innocence of the dove is praiseworthy if one were to take either of them on its own. But the disposition blended from the middle of the two becomes virtue. One who falls short in self-control is licentious. One who goes to excess has his conscience seared, as the Apostle defines it. The first is shamelessly poured out in pleasures, while the second loathes marriage as much as adultery. The disposition found between these is self-control. As the Lord says, this world lies in the power of the evil one, and what opposes virtue, which is wickedness, is foreign to those who follow the law. So whoever journeys through this world in this life will safely complete this necessary journey of virtue if he keeps to the true highway, the road worn smooth and whitened by virtue, and never turns aside through vice into the trackless places beside it. But, as has been said, the adversary's plotting rises along with the ascent of virtue and finds for each person the occasions suited to him for turning aside to evil. So at that time, when the people had grown greater in the godly life, the adversary took up another plot. He acted like men skilled in war who see that a frontal battle against a stronger force is hard to win, and so outmanoeuvre the enemy with tricks and ambushes. In the same way the army of vice no longer brings its forces out face to face against those strengthened by law and virtue, but carries out its plot in secret through ambushes. It therefore calls in sorcery as an ally against those it plots against. The history says that this sorcerer was a seer and augur who had, from some working of demons, a power that could harm his opponents. The ruler of the Midianites hired him to harm by curses those who live for God, but he turned the curse into a blessing. Following the sequence of what we have already considered, we understand this to mean that even sorcery has no power against those who live in virtue, and that those who are nourished by divine help prevail over every plot.

The history testifies that the man in question practised divination by augury. It says that he had the instruments of divination in hand and took counsel from birds. Before this, it says that he was taught about the business before him by the braying of the donkey. Because he was accustomed, through some demonic working, to take counsel from the cries of irrational animals, Scripture told of the donkey's sound as articulate speech. It shows that those already in the grip of this kind of demonic deceit go so far as to accept as speech the teaching they draw from the cries of irrational animals by some sort of observation. Paying attention to it, he was taught through the very things by which he was deceived that the power he had been hired to oppose was invincible. In the gospel history, too, the gathered band of demons called Legion was drawn up to resist the authority of the Lord. But when the one who has power over all drew near, it cried out his surpassing power and did not hide the truth that he is the divine nature, who will bring punishment on sinners at the appointed times. For the voice of the demons says, 'We know who you are, the Holy One of God,' and, 'You have come before the time to torment us.' The same thing happened then too: the demonic power attending the seer taught Balaam that the people could not be fought or resisted. Fitting the history to what we examined earlier, we say that whoever wished to curse those living in virtue could utter no grievous or unseemly word, but would turn the curse into a blessing. The meaning is this: the stain of reproach does not touch those who live according to virtue. How will someone who owns nothing be reproached for greed? How will anyone spread talk of debauchery about someone who lives withdrawn and apart, or of anger about the gentle, or of conceit about the humble? How will anyone blame for any other fault those who are known for its opposite? Their aim is to live a life that gives blame no hold, so that, as the Apostle says, the opponent may be put to shame, having nothing to say. That is why the man hired to curse says, 'How shall I curse one whom the Lord does not curse?' That is: How shall I reproach one who has given no handle [?] for reproach, whose life cannot be wounded by vice because he looks to God? The inventor of vice failed in this, but he did not stop scheming against those he was plotting against altogether. Instead he turned his scheming to his own favourite hold and once again lured nature into evil through pleasure. Pleasure is truly set out like bait for every vice, and it easily draws greedy [?] souls onto the hook of destruction. Above all, nature is swept off its guard into evil through licentious pleasure. And this is what happened then too. For those who had overcome arms, who had shown every assault of iron to be weaker than their own strength, and who had routed the enemy's battle line by force, to the

[?] ... anger hinted at. After all this he comes to the mountain of rest. He does not set foot on the land below, which the people below looked toward because of the promise. He no longer tastes earthly food, for he had learned to live on the food that flows down from above. He went up to the very summit of the mountain, like a skilled sculptor who has carved the whole statue of his own life, and at the exact peak of his work he set not an end but a crowning top. For what does the history say of him? 'Moses the servant of the Lord died by the word of God, and no one knew his burial place; his eyes were not dimmed, and his face was not corrupted.' From this we learn that after so many achievements he was then found worthy of this lofty name and called the servant of God. That is the same as saying that he had become superior to everything, for no one could serve God without having become superior to everything in the world. For him this was also the goal of the virtuous life, achieved through the word of God. The history calls it death, but it is a living death. No grave follows it and no mound is heaped over it, and it brings neither dimness to the eyes nor corruption to the face. What, then, do we learn from what has been said? To look to one goal throughout life: to be called the servant of God because of the way we have lived. You must overcome all your enemies: the Egyptian, the Amalekite, the Idumean, the Midianite. You must cross the water and be illumined [?] by the cloud, be sweetened by the wood, drink from the rock and taste the food from above. Through purity and chastity you must make your own way up the mountain, and once there be instructed in the divine mystery by the sound of the trumpets. In the darkness that is hard to see into you must draw near to God through faith, and there be taught the mysteries of the tabernacle and the dignity of the priesthood. You must become the stonecutter of your own heart, so that the divine words are engraved on it by God. You must destroy the golden idol, that is, wipe out from your life the desire to have more. You must be raised so high that you prove invincible against the sorcery of Balaam. When you hear 'sorcery', think of the many-sided deceit of this life, by which people, as if drugged by a cup of Circe, abandon their own nature and are reshaped into the forms of irrational animals. When you have passed through all of this, the rod of the priesthood blossoms in you. It draws no moisture from the earth to make it bud, but has the power to bear fruit from within, and its fruit is a nut, bitter and astringent at first touch but sweet and good to eat inside. And when everything that rises against your dignity is destroyed, swallowed into the earth like Dathan or consumed by fire like Korah, then you will draw near to the goal. By goal I mean that for whose sake everything is done. The goal of farming is enjoying the harvest. The goal of building a house is living in it. The goal of trade is wealth. And the goal of the labours of the contests

is the crown. In the same way the goal of the lofty way of life is to be called the servant of God. Along with this comes not being buried under a mound, which means that one's life becomes bare and free of the burden of evil things dragged along behind it. The text gives another mark of this service: the eye was not dimmed and the face was not corrupted. For how could an eye that is always in the light be dimmed by the darkness to which it is a stranger? And one who has achieved incorruption throughout his whole life admits no corruption at all into himself. Whoever has truly been made in the image of God and has never turned aside from the divine stamp bears its marks in himself. He agrees in every way, by likeness, with the archetype, and adorns his own soul with what is incorruptible, unchangeable and untouched by any evil. These are the things, man of God, Caesarius, that this brief discourse of ours sets before you about the perfection of the virtuous life. It has sketched the life of the great Moses as a kind of original model of beauty, so that each of us, by imitating his way of life, may copy into ourselves the features of the beauty that has been shown to us. That Moses reached the perfection that is possible is shown by the divine voice, and what more trustworthy witness could we find? It says to him, 'I have known you above all.' He was also called the friend of God by God himself. He chose to perish along with everyone else rather than see the Divine refuse in its kindness to be reconciled to them for their offences. So he stopped God's wrath against the Israelites, and God changed his own judgement so as not to grieve his friend. All such things are clear testimony and proof that the life of Moses climbed to the highest limit of perfection. What we set out to find was the perfection of the virtuous life, and what has been said has shown us what that perfection is. So it is time for you, my noble friend, to look to the model. Take what has been seen through a higher interpretation of the events told in the history and carry it over into your own life, so that you may be known by God and become his friend. For this is truly perfection. It is not to keep away from a life of vice out of slavish fear of punishment. Nor is it to do good in the hope of rewards, trading in the virtuous life with the attitude of a merchant striking a bargain. It is to look beyond everything, even the things laid up in hope through the promises, and to regard only one thing as fearful, falling from God's friendship, and only one thing as precious and desirable, becoming God's friend. This, in my judgement, is the perfection of life. Whatever you may find as your mind is lifted toward what is more magnificent and more divine, and much [?] . . . will be found . . . [?] and the dominion forever and ever. Amen.
